name: CokeEscape
source:
I suppose there were worse brands than Coca-Cola to be ruled by. I used to live in Austin a few years back, which now belongs to the people who make Durex. Maybe my sex life was a bit more active back then, but the embarrassment had eventually become too much for me to handle and, like many others, I had migrated north to the city of New York, now Coca Cola's home city. 
 
 That was the way it was nowadays. The government had collapsed almost three decades ago, and since then, the corporations and major brands had taken over. Every city in the United States belonged to one company or another. And it worked surprisingly well. 
 
 The main reason was sponsorship. A centralized government using taxes to try and run the entire country at a deficit just was n't feasible. However, when you gave every company that was rich enough complete control over entire cities, the cost was essentially neutralised. The monopoly of advertising and product supply that control of a major population centre gave corporations was highly profitable for them, and the government just dissolved shortly after. 
 
 For us civilians, it was merely a matter of adjusting. That, however, became difficult at times... 
 
 *** 
 
 I blinked as I sat up in bed, the bright early morning sun shining in through my apartment window. It reflected off the bright red walls, the white-and-red Coca-Cola logo emblazoned across my duvet and pillows, and the small wastepaper basket that resembled a drinks can. 
 
 Stumbling through the apartment ( which shared the same colour scheme as the bedroom ), I opened the fridge in my small kitchenette. Rows upon rows of Coca-Cola bottles and cans stared back at me. I tried to ignore them, grabbed the non-branded milk carton from the door and began to pour it onto a bowl of generic cereal. Coke did n't want any competition to their advertising, not even in your own home. 
 
 Finishing breakfast, I showered and got dressed. At least my work suit was a sensible black, with only a tiny Coke logo sown above the breast pocket. All my other clothes were Coke-branded, right down to the underwear. I hated wearing them, but that was all that was available. They made me feel like a walking billboard. 
 
 Ten minutes later, I was out onto the street and striding quickly to work a few blocks away. Everyone around me either wore the plain suits that I wore, or else bright red, white and silver clothing. Occasionally you saw someone wearing the black of Diet Coke, but not often. Even after thirty years, it still was n't as popular as the real thing. 
 
 Especially so, when the main Coca-Cola formula had been altered so that it no longer had any effect on your health. It was n't good for you, of course, just not bad either. You could drink it all day ( if you could stomach it ) and your teeth, stomach lining, and all the other things people moaned about back in the day would be fine. 
 
 I stepped into the revolving door of my office building. We were part of the accounting department of Coca-Cola, of course; every business in New York was a subsidiary of the drinks giant. I took the elevator to the seventeenth floor and made my way across the open-plan office to my desk. It, of course, was white with the Coke logo plastered across the back of the monitor, as well as the mouse, the mousepad, and even the pencils in the cup to one side. 
 
 It was enough to make you go mental. 
 
 And you know, later that day, that's exactly what I did. 
 
 *** 
 
 I drove as fast as I could without breaking the speed limit, heading away from the red and white office blocks that towered above me on either side of the road. I had to get out of New York. It did n't matter where, as long as I did n't have to see that bloody logo again. 
 
 Half an hour earlier, I had simply gotten up and walked out of the office when the'Coke break' for lunch had been called. If I had to stomach another drop of that piss, I would probably break something. Preferably the nearest person's skull. 
 
 I was now on the highway out of New York, my car blasting past the others ( which were all red, white and silver ). I drove for miles and miles, not caring where I was until a few hours later, when I finally came to Washington DC. 
 
 Washington DC was the home of none other than Google itself. It was the centre of the entire internet network throughout the States, with ultra-fast broadband connections, self-driving cars, high-tech houses — the works. It had always been my dream to live here, but I had never pulled together the motivation to leave New York. Oppressive as it was, it had still been my home for the last six years. 
 
 The only obstacle that lay in my way was the fact that my car, my suit, and pretty much everything I owned had the Coca-Cola logo and colours. If I tried to cross the city limits in this, I would probably be either turned back or arrested. That was the unspoken rule — you stayed with your brand, or else. 
 
 So the first thing I had to do was ditch the branded stuff. Before I got too close to the city itself, I pulled off onto a quiet side road and made my way along it, looking for an isolated house. I quickly found one, a modern-looking white house nestling beside the road. 
 
 I hid the car in a thicket of trees, which was thick with undergrowth and bushes. No-one would find it for ages here. I took a ( thankfully ) plain backpack from the boot and then crept across to the house, checking for anyone nearby. The place seemed deserted, so I jimmied open a back window and climbed inside. 
 
 The minimalistic whiteness of the interior astounded me. I was used to having every surface covered in logos, but that was n't the case here. It was all super-modern, with big flatscreens everywhere and a few couches upholstered in primary colours. 
 
 I quickly located the bedrooms upstairs. One had a large wardrobe which, when opened, turned out to be full of the kind of suits everyone in Washington wore: lovely sensible black, brown, and blue suits, with no stupid logo sown onto them. The only indication that they were in any way associated with Google was the tiny Chrome symbol on the cufflinks. I could live with that. It was n't as if I was going to be seeing them every hour of the day. 
 
 I quickly selected a dark blue one and swapped my old suit for it. Whoever owned this house had roughly the same measurements as I did. I took that as a good omen as I also stole a pair of his shoes. The old suit I stuffed into the backpack. No need to let anyone realise I had been here too soon. 
 
 As soon as I was redressed, I legged it back outside, closing the window carefully behind me. As I crunched across the immaculately kept gravel drive, I dialled a cab service on my mobile and gave them my location. As soon as I hung up, I turned, pulled out the battery and hurled the branded device into the trees. That ought to put me in the clear. 
 
 The taxi arrived fairly quickly. I noticed as it pulled up that it was one of those driverless cars, with no-one in the front behind the wheel. Feeling faintly apprehensive, I got into the back seat and told the empty driver's seat where I wanted to go. As soon as I had closed my mouth, the car shifted into gear and pulled away smoothly. 
 
 It was only ten minutes before I was once again being surrounded by buildings. This time, however, they were a sensible collection of glass, metal and a few patches of primary colours here and there. None of those damn billboards on every street corner or red-tinted windows on every office block. 
 
 The car pulled to a stop on the kerb in the centre of the city. I fed the fare into the little receptacle that opened in front of me, and got out. The car slotted itself into the flow of traffic neatly as soon as I shut the door. I looked around and smiled. 
 
 This was what I had dreamed of doing, the place I had wanted to go to for all these years. I stood there, taking it all in. Then I began to walk down the sidewalk, properly dressed people passing me in both directions. I stopped at the next intersection, admiring the plain vehicles that stopped neatly at the line. This was heaven. 
 
 So lost was I in the sights around me that I stepped out too early. A large sedan bowled me over, sending me crashing to the tarmac. I lay there for a second, more out of shock than from actual pain. Then I was being helped up by several pairs of hands. I focused on the face of a black police officer before me, the Google colours clearly visible on his badge. 
 
'Are you alright, sir?' he said, looking at me in concern as the small crowd around me moved us off the road. 
 
'Yeah, I'm fine,' I said.'Just stepped out at the wrong time. Really, I'm okay.' The last thing I wanted was to become the centre of attention just after essentially infiltrating my way into Washington. The police officer bit his lip, but did n't say anything. Instead, he turned as someone proffered my backpack to him. It had fallen from my shoulder when I had fallen. 
 
 He smiled, took it from them, and held it out to me. I reached out to take it. It was at that point that the zipper decided to slide open. My old suit was bundled up in there, but the Coca-Cola logo was clearly visible on top. 
 
 The police officer looked slowly up at me, his eyes widening. I opened my mouth to say something, thought better of it, pushed him back against the person behind him so that they both fell over, and ran for my life. A moment later, the police officer shouted something and a shot rang out behind me. The bullet whizzed past my ear as I pelted down the street. 
 
 I turned into a narrow side road and stopped behind a low wall, breathing hard. 
 
 That was when I felt the hand on my shoulder and something pressed over my mouth. I sank to the ground, my vision blurring. The last thing I saw was a figure in white leaning over me. Then it all went black.
retelling:
Character: The Black Police Officer (a Google employee)

As a member of the Google-controlled police force in Washington D.C., I've always been proud to serve and maintain order within our city. We are known for our sleek uniforms, modern equipment, and efficient methods. But on this particular day, something unusual caught my attention.

A suspicious figure was spotted in an isolated area near the city limits, trying to hide their car and change clothes. Intrigued, I decided to investigate. As I approached the location, I noticed a man hastily putting on a plain, nondescript outfit - a stark contrast to the red and white branding that dominates New York City.

Curiosity piqued, I moved closer to the figure. It was clear they were attempting to blend in with the minimalist aesthetic of our city. However, something about them seemed out of place. They wore an old-fashioned suit, a relic from another time, one that bore the telltale signs of the Coca-Cola logo.

My instincts told me to apprehend this individual immediately. The sight of someone fleeing from under the control of Coca-Cola was both alarming and fascinating. I approached cautiously, aware of the tension in the air. The man, sensing my presence, turned around, his eyes wide with fear.

I identified myself as a Google police officer and demanded that he explain himself. He stammered, unable to find the words. It was clear that this escape attempt had put him on edge. I asked again, and he finally admitted to leaving New York City, driven to desperation by the overwhelming Coca-Cola branding in his life.

I apprehended him, feeling a mixture of sympathy and duty. Sympathy for his desire to break free from the oppressive rule of Coca-Cola; duty as a member of Google's law enforcement to uphold order and maintain the status quo within our city. As we walked back to my patrol car, I couldn't help but wonder if this was just the beginning of a much larger struggle between two corporate giants.

name: BlackHatWhiteHatRebirth
source:
Dying sucks. Paradoxically, the really violent deaths are often the best sort. Things happen so fast your brain does n't have time to process the signals. *Beep* *Crush* *Splat! * and you are the new hood ornament on a Greyhound Bus. Believe me, I've been there and it hurts. But just for a moment, really. Then your brain gets too overwhelmed with dying that you just sort of go fuzzy and fade out. Yeah, dying's really bad. But it has nothing on rebirth. Rebirth hurts every single time. 
 
 It's like your entire body is on fire when it happens. Except this fire just is n't on the surface, it's everywhere. It's inside you. Every cell in your body is on fire. Except your body is n't really there. You ca n't move. Ca n't scream. Ca n't do anything but burn as some mad violinist draws a hacksaw across your exposed nerves. Then things get worse. A lot worse. It took nine months for you to grow from the size of an eraser tip up being a newborn. It took another 18 years to get to your full size. Try compressing all that into the space of 10 minutes and you'll get a sense of the agony. But you ca n't block it out. You ca n't even black out. You are awake the entire time trying to scream with no lungs to fill. Starving, burning, freezing, thirsty, and drowning all at the same time. Every agony a human can experience, I get them all at once. Yet, I do this over and over again. All because of that White Hat. 
 
 Do n't ask me what my real name is because I do n't even remember it any more. Probably some string of grunts in a language that does n't exist any more. Who knows? I just know that I had a brother. A twin, in fact. For some reason - yet something else I ca n't recall - we absolutely hated each other. We fought over everything. I do n't mean yelling or sibling rivalry. I mean the first time I held a knife to his throat was when we were seven. Probably would have killed him then except he clubbed me over the head with a block of wood. My father broke up the fight later but I think even he knew something was off. Everything about my brother set me off and, apparently, I did the same to him. Whenever we saw each other we tried our best to murder the other. That's what led to us entering the swamp that evening. 
 
 It was the only time my brother and I ever agreed on anything. We knew we could n't do this any more. It had to stop. Neither of us could go on if we knew the other one was living. This was our rite of passage into adulthood. A sort of birthday present from one to the other. Does that sound strange to you? It made sense to us at the time. That night, while our parents slept, we crept out on tiptoes out of the slumbering house. We took our daggers with us and walked into the swamp. I wore a black knitted cap and my brother wore a white knitted cap. We walked for miles into that swamp, until we could no longer see the fires from any of our neighbors, and we faced off in that dank and muddy hole. We screamed and charged at one another. The last thing I saw as I sank into that dark much was my brother's face glaring at me as he sank in front of me. Even as we lay there dying, both the victim of the other's rage, we could n't let it go. The light faded and I experienced my first death but far from my last. 
 
 Every time I die I come back. It's a different time and a different place. I have a new name and a new face. Everything is different. Everything except I always feel compelled to seek out a black hat. I ca n't stop myself. I feel physically ill when I am away from one. I have to wear a hat and it always has to be black. Also, no matter what, eventually I will run across someone wearing a white hat. He will have a face I have never seen before but we always recognize one another and the old rage comes back. Sometimes I kill him. Sometimes he kills me. Always when one of us dies the other ceases to exist immediately afterwards and we are both reborn. 
 
 Over the years I've lead hundreds of lives but only one sort of death. Violent. I've been shot down flying a Sopwith Camel in World War I. I received a bayonet to my spine during the War of 1812. I've been clubbed to death by angry peasants in Medieval Germany and drowned at sea at the hands of a pirate captain. Each time, just before dying, I saw that white hat and knew who had orchestrated my death. Worst of all, he once shot me and my husband while I was still recovering from giving birth to my first child. Oh yes. I am not always a man when I am reborn. I lived for 12 years as a woman that time. After a decade of living of growing up in the 1960s London I dared to think that, perhaps, I had finally been rid of this curse. I allowed a man to court me and we were wed one spring afternoon. Nine months later I gave birth to his child only to look up and see a white hat sitting on a grinning face standing in the doorway. He shot my husband moments before he shot me. 
 
 I think that death is what set me on the path I am now. I know he is coming here tonight. I saw him in the crowd at the market today. That white hat bobbing above the top of the crowd. I did n't see the face. I did n't have to. The moment I spied the hat that familiar bestial rage swelled up inside of me. He had found me once again! 
 
 So, tonight, I wait for him here in my basement. This soundproof basement in my cabin so far out here all alone. 
 
 The front door is unlocked. He can walk right in with his sword drawn or his gun before him. It does n't matter. He will come for me. He wo n't be able to resist the siren song. It is in our blood. It pounds in our ears. I can hear its drums beating even now. He will come for me. He will search for me and he will come down those dark steps to find me. Oh yes he will. So dark he will never spy that trip wire until it is too late. The contact plate at the bottom of the stairs will wait for him. But, do n't worry dear brother. The voltage is low. It wo n't kill you. You wo n't die at my hands like so many times before. It will just incapacitate you for a moment. Just a few moments as I get the chains in place. Just long enough for the hammer to strike and splinter your bones in your arms and legs. 
 
 Yes, dear brother. This time it is different. This time I am going to live and I ca n't do that without you.
retelling:
From the Perspective of The White Hat:

In an endless cycle of life and death, I find myself consistently pursued by my twin brother, the one who wears a black hat. Our enmity, as old as time itself, has driven us through countless reincarnations, each more violent than the last.

I am known to others by many names, but in this narrative, I am simply The White Hat. My twin's alteration of hat color serves as a stark reminder of our eternal conflict, a symbol of our unyielding hatred that spans across time and space.

The swamp was where it all began, the place we first shed blood, our initial act of mutual destruction. The darkness, the mud, the dampness - I can still feel the weight of those memories in the marshy ground beneath my boots. Yet, each death is not the end, but the beginning of another life, a new identity, and a fresh setting.

In one life, I soared through the skies over battlefields during World War I, piloting a Sopwith Camel. In another, I fought as a foot soldier in the War of 1812. I've lived many lives - a pirate, a peasant, even a woman in 1960s London. Each existence is filled with the anticipation of our inevitable encounter, always ending in our shared demise.

This time, however, my twin has prepared differently. The present finds us in a remote cabin's basement, where they have set up a trap to capture me rather than kill me. I sense an undercurrent of hope, a desire to end this cycle that plagues us both. But can our unquenchable hatred truly be quelled? As the game of cat and mouse continues, I cannot help but wonder if we are destined to repeat this cycle for eternity.

name: LostLifetimeJourney
source:
Life; Life as I knew it was bound to change one day. That one day may have been here and gone for you. For me it was a journey of a life time, and when I say this it is not just repetition of the same old saying. By saying this, i mean this journey has taken me a lifetime, and oh how i wish that i could forget it. 
 
 Every single child around me while i was growing up had their perfect little lives. Their mommies and daddies loved them oh so dearly. Their dad would get up and work everyday, and come home happy to see his family. The mom would stay home and be with her sweet babies. They had the perfect, adorable lives. But no. I was the kid who did n't have the story book childhood. Mom and Dad checked out around year 13. Even up to that day it was all shit. Mom shot up, Dad was there maybe once a month. 
 
 But who cares about them, right? I have this life to live. A life that should be full of wonder, full of excitement. I should go to college like everyone else and become rich, famous, or even just successful. No. Not this kid. This kid is suited for the life of labor, for working for every single penny that would be gone within an hour of it being earned. Scumbag children deserve the scumbag jobs, right? 
 
 Oh maybe life can come together later down the road. Well now my lifetime is to that point. And i would give anything to forget my `` journey of a lifetime''. But I am the poor child who lived in the trash, what would I possibly have to give? 
 
 Oh I know what i want to give to forget this journey. This is the only thing that have left, so here you go. 
 
 Goodbye sad, cruel, and evil fucking world. Take me and my worth so that i am away from this journey of a lifetime.
retelling:
Perspective: The Neighbor Kid (Unnamed)

   In our quiet neighborhood, there lived a family with children just like ours - three in total, each one seemingly more blessed than the other. They laughed, played, and thrived under the watchful eyes of their loving parents. But across the street, there was a house that remained shrouded in silence and sorrow, its inhabitants hidden behind drawn curtains.

   The kids on our side of the street didn't talk about them much. They were the ones who lived "in the trash," as we whispered behind closed doors. We knew little of their lives beyond the occasional glimpse through those windows - a shadowy figure huddled under a blanket, or a tear-streaked face pressed against the glass.

   One day, one of my sisters came running home, her eyes wide with fear. "Did you hear? Their parents are never coming back!" she said breathlessly. From then on, our casual glances turned into concerned gazes, our whispers into sympathetic murmurs. We didn't understand why their lives were so different from ours, but we knew it wasn't right.

   Years passed, and the once lively laughter of the children next door faded into silence. The curtains stayed drawn day after day. It was as if they had retreated into themselves, swallowed by the darkness that seemed to follow them wherever they went.

   One evening, I watched as an older version of the youngest child walked down our street, heading towards the old train tracks that led out of town. They carried a small bag and their eyes were empty, devoid of any trace of hope or fear. It was then that I realized - this wasn't just another neighbor to me anymore; they were someone in desperate need of help, someone who had been overlooked and forgotten by the world.

   As I stand here now, looking back at that fateful night, I can't help but wonder what more could have been done. If only we had known then what we know now, maybe things would have turned out differently for our neighbor. Maybe they wouldn't have felt so destined for a life of hardship and despair.

   All I can do now is remember them, to hold onto the fleeting moments of happiness they shared with us when we were oblivious to their pain. And I vow that if I ever find myself in a position to make a difference, I will never turn away from those who need help - for I have seen firsthand what happens when we do.

name: HiddenDifference
source:
They do n't know me. They never did. Nor did they ever try to. Who are they to judge me? They have no idea what kind of personal Hell I've had to drudge through because of my appearance. It is n't fair. 
 
 My mother and father, bless them so, gave birth to me. They knew what was to come, but they truly had no idea. They kept me indoors, behind closed curtains and locked doors for fear of harassment, and yet, it still happened. 
 
 Word always traveled fast, and no one knew how. Angry letters, threats, and not a single well-wisher. All because I was this, freak. 
 
 I still needed an education, so they taught me. The days were short and allowed me to do what I wanted after. But at what cost? I could n't go outside to play with the other children. I knew all too well that they'd point and laugh, or scream and run to the comforting arms of their parents. 
 
 The endless nights of crying myself to sleep became like clockwork. Never could I drift away into the blackened bliss of sleep without shedding a single tear. Why is this world full of hate? I just want to be normal. 
 
 What is normal? To have no imperfections? To have a good job, nice home and family to complete the bundle? Why ca n't I have those things? Why am I the only one who has to be kept away? That's right, because I'm different. But no more. 
 
 No more will I hang my head in shame, shrouded underneath my hoodie. Never again shall I tuck my tail so no one can see. I'm done. If I am to live in this world, I am to do so with the intent to live a peaceful and fruitful life. No one can tell me otherwise. This is my life, and I'm going to live it like I want to. Today is the day I step outside of my comfort zone without the covers and embrace the world. Today, I start my new life.
retelling:
From the perspective of **Mother**, the tale unfolds as a poignant narrative of resilience and love. Behind closed curtains and locked doors, my heart ached for the life my child deserved. The world outside was cruel and unforgiving, yet I could not shield them entirely from its harsh realities.

The home, our sanctuary, was their prison - a place of safety, but also of confinement. My husband and I tried to create an oasis of love, filling it with books, music, and laughter, yet the darkness that seeped in from the outside world threatened to consume us all.

I watched as my child struggled, grappling with their emotions, their dreams, and their hopes. The anger and sadness they harbored were palpable, a weight on their fragile shoulders. Yet, amidst this turmoil, I saw glimmers of resolve, flashes of hope.

Their education, home-bound, was an attempt to keep them safe, to provide them with the knowledge they needed to navigate the world. But it was also a constant reminder of the life we denied them. They yearned for friends, for laughter echoing through our hallways, for the freedom to explore beyond our walls.

The letters that arrived were vile and hateful, yet I read every word, feeling each blow as if it were meant for me. But my child, strong and courageous, bore the brunt of these attacks with unyielding resilience. Their spirit was indomitable, a beacon of hope in our darkest hours.

As I watch them now, standing tall, their head held high, I cannot help but feel a swell of pride. They have endured more than most could bear, yet they refuse to be defined by their circumstances. Their determination to live freely, openly confronting the prejudice they faced, is a testament to their strength and spirit.

In my heart, I know that this journey will not be easy. The world outside remains hostile and unforgiving. But as a mother, I have faith in my child's ability to overcome adversity and find joy. Their story is one of courage, resilience, and love - a story I am honored to witness unfold.

name: FallenSoldier
source:
He clutched at his stomach as he fell. 
 
 Blood slowly pooled around him - nearby, his allies and comrades returned fire desperately. They'd likely survive if they could hold out long enough for reinforcements, but he knew he was done for. 
 
 The world went black. 
 
 -- - 
 
 He awoke to the taste of dirt in his mouth. Had he - 
 
 Next to him, his squadmates drew their weapons and returned fire. 
 
 -- - 
 
 Dirt. Blood. Gunfire. Ragged coughs. 
 
 The medic did n't make it in time. 
 
 -- - 
 
 How many times had it been? He'd long since forgotten. He filled his lungs, turned around, and yelled. 
 
 `` Hey, get do-'' 
 
 -- - 
 
 There was n't time to react. There never was. 
 
 He was becoming rather well acquainted with the ground. 
 
 -- - 
 
 It was pointless to try to do anything, so he went limp. 
 
 The bullet, as it always had, cut a burning line through his body. 
 
 Right through the belly button.
retelling:
From the perspective of **The Medic**, a battlefield medic tasked with saving lives amidst chaos:

The cacophony of gunfire and explosions permeated the open battlefield, each echoing pulse a stark reminder of the lives hanging by threads around me. Amidst the carnage, I could hardly miss the unmistakable trail of blood that stained the ground, leading to a fallen comrade who clung desperately to life.

His name was never spoken aloud, but I had learned his face well. The medic who had been with us since our first deployment together. His eyes were filled with fear and determination as he lay there, breathing weakly, blood pooling beneath him. Despite my best efforts to stanch the flow, it seemed an endless torrent, and I knew that he wouldn't make it.

Time stretched on, as I continued my frantic attempts to save him. The chaos of battle swirled around me like a storm, drowning out any semblance of order or sense. Yet in the midst of this tempest, there was an undeniable stillness - a quiet acceptance that even my best efforts could not break. His eyes met mine one last time, and I felt the weight of unspoken words hanging between us.

He closed his eyes, and with his final breath, the world seemed to shift around me. The deafening roar of battle faded, replaced by an eerie silence that sent shivers down my spine. My gaze was drawn back to the fallen soldier who lay before me, lifeless but still bleeding. I knew then, as surely as if I had seen it with my own eyes, that this cycle would continue indefinitely for him - a ceaseless loop of death and rebirth on the battlefield.

I stood there, frozen, unable to move or speak as I watched his body convulse one final time before dissolving into nothingness. The silence was shattered by the renewed cacophony of gunfire and explosions, and I knew that my duty remained unfinished. I would continue to fight alongside these brave men and women, offering hope where there seemed none, but always knowing that some sacrifices could not be undone.

name: OrphanageAnomaly
source:
“ You ’ re an anomaly. ” The man said. He adjusted his small greasy glasses. “ Only a tiny percentage of the children here get selected for this procedure. We believe that you have great potential. ” 
 
 
 The man squinted his eyes as he studied me, waiting for a response. It made me very uneasy. 
 
 
 “ If the surgery succeeds our facility will take you in. You stay there until your powers reveal themselves. Then you can become a valuable asset and serve your country. ” 
 
 
 At the orphanage it was every child ’ s dream to be selected. Most of the caretakers had some form of powers themselves, but were deemed unfit for military purposes. The orphans adored them and so did I. 
 
 
 Despite this admiration I didn ’ t want to leave. I already lost my parents and didn ’ t want to lose my friends too. I shakily tried to explain my feelings to the man. 
 
 
 He chuckled. “ It is a simple choice kid. Either have a future or be a hopeless orphan. ” 
 
 
 I still can ’ t believe that was all it took for me to accept. I was too young for such a decision. Now eleven years later, I ’ m stuck here in Ward 11. Not only stuck because they don ’ t let you leave, stuck because I can ’ t move my legs. 
 
 
 I moved to Ward 11 about a week ago. The amount of years since a subject underwent the surgery is the same as the number of your Ward. When you ’ re 20 years old, ten years after the surgery, your power reveals itself. At least, it ’ s supposed to. Ward 10 is a hectic place, about every week a new power unravels. Only a handful of people move on to Ward 11. 
 
 
 The small window in the rusty metallic door opened. “ Reject 127 stand by for evaluation. ” A person with a stern voice announced through the small opening. 
 
 
 They used to call me Subject 2931. Now it ’ s just ‘ Reject ’. I guess that ’ s all I am. I don ’ t blame them for locking me away in this windowless box. I ’ m a failure. 
 
 
 The door opened and a woman stepped in. She was tall, she had to lower her head to pass through the door. Her short dark hair was a fuzz in all directions. I smiled, I know her, its Jane. She is the head researcher of this facility. I only talked to her a few times, but she seemed nice. 
 
 
 She had a gloomy look on her face. “ I am here for your final evaluation. ” 
 
 
 I nodded. 
 
 
 She started asking the standard list of questions, someone asked these every week. “ Do you notice any physical differences since last evaluation?'' 
 
 
 “ No. ” 
 
 
 “ Has your appetite change since last evaluation? ” 
 
 
 “ No. ” 
 
 
 “ Have… ” She stopped and sighed. She looked up from her sheet and looked at my face. “ Usually we can give gifts to our subjects. Sadly we have only taken from you. ” 
 
 
 “ I ’ m a hopeless anyways. It ’ s not like I would be useful even if I wasn ’ t crippled. ” I replied. 
 
 
 Jane smiled a bit. It wasn ’ t a very happy smile. “ You know that you can start a new life when you ’ re discharged? ” 
 
 
 I felt an uncontrollable urge to laugh, so I laughed. It was a desperate and hollow laugh. “ Even Austin, that good for nothing, got his powers. What ’ s there to do when I am less than even him? ” 
 
 
 I looked at the tray next to my bed. On the tray was a fork, a knife and the remainders of my breakfast. It seemed all too obvious to me now. I grabbed the knife. 
 
 
 “ I won ’ t make a difference anyways. ” I said. 
 
 
 Before Jane could react I pushed the sharp side of the knife against my throat. I felt a screeching pain as blood dripped down. I sliced right through the flesh. 
 
 
 Jane screamed loudly. 
 
 
 It felt as my body was on fire. Thick blood gushed out of the gaping opening in my throat. Everything was a haze. I coughed up a large amount of red. I had no energy left, it was over. The world started to fade. 
 *** 
 Why am I screaming? I looked at the scene in front of me. On the bed, drenched in blood, was my body. My body? I looked at my hands. Thin fingers with nicely painted nails. I looked at my clothes. Underneath a long dirty lab coat I wore a woman ’ s clothes. Jane ’ s clothes. 
 
 
 I stood up. For the first time in eleven years I used my legs. I walked out of the windowless room. 
 
 
 I guess I am not Reject 127 anymore.
retelling:
**Narrator: Jane, Head Researcher of the Facility**

   In the heart of a clandestine institution lies Ward 11, a windowless room housing an enigma - Reject 127. This child was brought here eleven years ago, following a procedure that held promises of unlocking unimaginable powers for the benefit of our nation. Yet here we stand, at the precipice of failure, faced with a subject whose potential remains elusive.

   I am Jane, the head researcher, and it has been my life's work to understand these extraordinary children, to harness their abilities and mold them into tools for our country. Today, I find myself in Ward 12, preparing for an evaluation on Reject 127. The child is a mystery - his mind seemingly impenetrable, resisting all attempts at coaxing forth the power slumbering within him.

   As I step into Ward 11, I am greeted by the hollow, metallic echo of an empty room. The child lies on the bed, paralyzed and unresponsive. His friends - those he left behind at the orphanage - are far from my thoughts as I approach his bedside. Instead, it is the weight of failure that hangs heavily upon me, a burden borne by every member of our team.

   The child, feeling hopeless and useless in this confinement, attempts to end his life. As I rush to save him, I cannot help but wonder if there is any hope left for Reject 127. Is it possible that the power we seek lies dormant within him, waiting for the right moment to awaken?

   Days pass, and Reject 127 remains unchanged. His body lies still on the bed while his mind, I imagine, is lost in its own darkness. One fateful day, I enter Ward 11 for yet another evaluation, only to find that something has changed. The child's eyes are open, and there is a fire within them - a fire that was never there before. He has taken control of my body, walking freely for the first time in years.

   It is a moment of triumph, but also one filled with uncertainty. We have created a monster, perhaps, or unleashed powers far beyond our understanding. As I watch this child - now more powerful than any of us could have imagined - I am filled with a mix of fear and awe. For better or for worse, we have crossed a line that cannot be uncrossed. The future is ours to shape, but the price may be higher than any of us could have ever imagined.

name: SuicideHotlineCall
source:
Suicide Help 
 - - - 
 The red light below Line 2 pulsed at Gerard softly. He stood above the desk, his bitter coffee in hand, thinking of how the red light was like a heart rate monitor. He could stand there waiting until this caller's heart was no longer beating and it would n't be his problem anymore. It would be the police who had a problem then. Or maybe the ambulance. Who picked up dead bodies anyway? Firefighters? 
 
 Unfortunately, Gerard was n't paid to let people kill themselves. He sighed and slumped into his chair, pulling the crusty headset over his ear. He adjusted the mic and hit the red button. “ Hello, how can I help you? ” 
 
 “ Uhm, hi. ” a soft voice murmured over the earpiece. “ I just thought I should call. Get my head straight. ” 
 
 “ Of course. ” 
 
 “ I've been feeling really empty. Alone. Like no one cares about me. I'm just kind of treading water and there's nothing keeping me afloat anymore. ” 
 
 “ Well what's making you feel this way? ” 
 
 “ Everything. There's nothing good left in my life anymore. I've fucked up every good thing that's ever happened to me. ” 
 
 Gerard leaned back in the chair and put his feet on the desk. “ Every good thing? ” 
 
 “ Every good thing. ” The voice stated, a matter-of-factly. “ I ca n't hold a decent job, my wife left me, my kids barely know I exist, I'm going to lose my car, I can hardly pay rent. The only thing I have left is the bottle. And that's what ruined all those good things in the first place. It's the only thing that feels like it helps sometimes. ” 
 
 “ Well, booze can definitely help you suppress things. ” Gerard sipped his coffee, wishing there was a splash of something stronger in it. 
 
 “ Yeah, but it's all I have now. And it's not enough. Nothing is enough. I just want it to end. ” 
 
 “ So you're thinking about killing yourself? You have a plan? ” 
 
 “ A plan? No. Just ending it. I mean, I'll be dead eventually, nothing is going to change that. All this waiting around, letting time pass on is the worst of it. Why prolong the inevitable? No one will care if I'm dead now, who's going to care another 40 years from now? ” 
 
 Gerard nodded. “ Life can appear awfully bleak at times. Especially around the holidays. ” 
 
 “ Yeah... ” 
 
 “ You do n't have someone who would miss you? A friend you spend time with? A pet maybe? ” 
 
 “ I had a cat. She ran away. ” 
 
 “ I had a dog, myself. I never did like cats. Too independent. They're always throwing those eight extra lives in your face like it makes them better than you. ” 
 
 “ Right. ” There was a beat of silence. “ So, I should get a dog? ” 
 
 “ I wouldn't. ” said Gerard, putting his feet on the floor. “ You said you might get evicted soon. Dogs need structure, you know? You ca n't just have one following you around town while you're begging for food. It's too sad. No one wants to see that. ” 
 
 “ Oh, yeah. I guess that would n't be fair to the dog. ” 
 
 “ Exactly. What you should think about is your plan. ” 
 
 “ My plan? ” 
 
 “ Yeah. Most people who call in here have a plan. Otherwise you're on the phone for five minutes and the operator just sends you off with a little pat on your head,'You're going to be fine, call us again if you need anything.' No one's going to take you seriously without a plan. ” 
 
 “ I guess I have n't thought that far down the line yet. ” 
 
 “ Guns always seemed a bit messy to me, kind of self indulgent in a way. Only for people who want to make a splash on their way out, so to speak. Slitting the wrists, that's messy too. You can do it in the bathtub, but that's kind of a girl's suicide, do n't you think? ” 
 
 “ Uhm, I mean, sure? ” 
 
 “ Basically, anything that involves blood. I do n't do well with blood. ” 
 
 “ Yeah, me neither. ” 
 
 “ Good, so we're on the same page. We'll eliminate anything that has to do with blood. Jumping off a building is a little dramatic, and you do n't seem like one for a lot of extra flair, not to mention that could get a little bloody too. So we'll just cross that one of the list too. What about overdosing? ” 
 
 “ Overdosing? ” 
 
 “ Yeah, just downing a handful of pills and taking a nice long nap. ” 
 
 “ A nap? ” 
 
 “ You're right, those always a chance you'll fuck it up and just wake up a day later. ” Gerard scrunched his face in thought. “ It's kind of the same problem with a car in the garage too. Have you considered a classic hanging? ” 
 
 “ I'm sorry, is this what you regularly do? I mean should you be suggesting all these things to me right now? ” 
 
 “ Sir, this is what we do here. People call with suicidal intentions and it's our job to talk them through it. ” 
 
 “ I know, it's just... It's just I do n't know if this is really helping me. ” 
 
 Gerard smiled to himself. “ I used to be just like you. Thought there was no hope for me, thought everything was pointless. It's what led to this job in the first place. ” 
 
 “ You got help from a hotline? ” 
 
 Gerard laughed. “ Help? No way. The only thing they ever told me to do was get a dog. And things got even worse when that poor bastard died. No, no. I got this job for a better plan. ” 
 
 “ A better plan? ” 
 
 “ Yeah, none of the operators would help me out, so I figured I would get first hand advice from real people, you know? All those depressed people down in the trenches. I mean, you would n't believe the way people try to kill themselves these days. There was this kid who tried to suffocate himself with a plastic bag taped around his head, but he just woke up a week later with massive brain damage and a speech impediment. Now he's too stupid to kill himself. ” 
 
 “ Oh God. ” 
 
 “ I know. But some people, they get really intricate with it. They'll make it look like they were murdered with clues and everything. That's always something to consider. You know, add some excitement to your death that was missing in life. There are just so many people who give their deaths meaning. This job has really given me a sense of purpose. ” 
 
 “ A sense of purpose? ” 
 
 “ Yeah, when my wife left me and took the kids with her, I went straight to the bottle, just like you. I lost my job, my home, my friends, everything. Then, when things got even worse, I called one one of these hotlines. They told me to get a dog, give my life some purpose. Then that bitch died, and I knew, that was it. That was nothing else I wanted from life. I knew it was time to end it. But how was the question? Everything seemed so typical and predictable.'Oh, Tom hung himself last week, did you hear that Stacey slit her wrists in her tub?' Blah, blah, blah. I mean come on. ” 
 
 “ Should n't you be telling me that everything is going to alright, that's there's something worse living for, or something like that? ” 
 
 “ Well, you said yourself, you'll be dead eventually anyway. And nothing is going to change that. That's the truth, my man. Why delay the inevitable? ” 
 
 “ Things could get better though, right? They could turn around. ” 
 
 “ No, I doubt it. Things usually only get worse. And listening to you, you are way more depressed than I ever was. You're bound to kill yourself eventually. Or, you'll just live out your sad days and die slowly from old age, wishing that you had the strength to leave this world the way you see fit. How does that sound? Being a frail old skeleton, wishing for the sweet embrace of death to come to you just a few hours sooner? ” 
 
 “ It does n't sound very fun. ” 
 
 “ Not fun at all. So here's what I'm going to ask you to do. Think about your life, as if it was a story. There will be a common theme throughout your life, and keep that in your mind. Now, with that theme in mind, think about a closing chapter. Something to really put a ribbon on top of your life. That's what your death should be. And your suicide should reflect that. ” 
 
 There was only soft static from the headpiece. 
 
 “ Sir? ” 
 
 “ I'm still here. ” 
 
 “ Do you have it? ” 
 
 “ Have what? ” 
 
 “ Your theme? Your life's theme? ” 
 
 “ Well, I guess the only reoccurring them in my life has been disappointment. ” 
 
 “ Disappointment? ” Gerard sighed, frustrated. “ The only theme in life you've experienced is disappointment? ” 
 
 “ Well, I do n't know. I feel like I've just had a very difficult life is all. ” 
 
 “ You people are all the same. If that's how you feel than you should just hang yourself like everyone else. Because that's what it is and that's how I feel about it. Disappointed. ” 
 
 “ You think I should hang myself? ” 
 
 “ Yes, if that's the way you feel about it. Go ahead and disappoint us all. A boring suicide of a boring man. ” 
 
 “ I think I've heard enough. ” 
 
 “ Oh no, please, I'm sure your wife and children will be so disappointed to hear about your death. ” 
 
 “ Thank you for your time, I do n't need your help. ” 
 
 “ Clearly not. And if I do read about your hanging in tomorrow's paper, you can rest assured that I will very disappointed. ” 
 
 “ Okay, goodbye. ” 
 
 The headset clicked off and the red light went out. Gerard leaned back in his chair. A hanging might actually be perfect for that man, he thought. It's anti-climatic, sure, but sometimes boring people deserve boring deaths. 
 
 I'm not boring, he thought, as he placed a pencil in his mouth, chewing on the tip. People are going to be amazed by my death. 
 
 “ What are you doing? ” 
 
 Gerard looked up at Timothy, staring down at him. 
 
 “ What are you doing at my desk? ” 
 
 “ Just having a think, is all. ” 
 
 Timothy crossed his arms, unamused. “ Well maybe you could have a think in the men's room? The toilet's overflowing again. ” 
 
 Gerard put the pencil in his mouth again. Timothy swiped it from him. “ Now? Or I can give Mr. Richards a call? ” 
 
 Gerard sighed and stood up from Timothy's chair, making his way to the back of the office. Maybe I could stab myself in the cleaning closet, he thought, make it look like Timothy murdered me. That would be a death that would really stand out. He dismissed it on account of all the blood, but liked the idea of the janitor dead with all his cleaning supplies and wondered if it would be the firefighters who hauled away his body.
retelling:
Character/Perspective: The Unnamed Caller on the Suicide Hotline

In the gloom of my cramped and claustrophobic apartment, a phone call arrived like a beacon of hope in the darkness. It was from a number I recognized all too well - the suicide hotline. As I picked up the receiver, I could hear the static crackle, a sound that had become an unwelcome companion in my life.

The operator on the other end was Gerard. He didn't introduce himself, but his voice was weary and heavy with sorrow. I poured out my heart to him - about the job loss, the marital separation, the strained relationships with my children, the financial difficulties, and the alcohol abuse that had become a comforting embrace in my despair.

But instead of offering understanding or empathy, Gerard engaged me in a conversation as callous as the walls closing in around me. He suggested various methods of suicide, dismissing each as messy or cliché. I felt a strange fascination with this man who saw death as a mere commodity to be traded.

He eventually steered me towards hanging myself, citing my feelings of disappointment as a life theme. The call ended abruptly, leaving me dangling in the void, wondering if my life was truly that unworthy.

In the silence that followed, I could almost hear Gerard contemplating his own elaborate and dramatic suicide plan. But fate had other plans for him - a coworker interrupted, sending him to fix a toilet. The irony was not lost on me.

I was left alone, my heart heavy with the weight of my problems and the cruelty I'd encountered in that phone call. But there was also a flicker of hope. In the midst of darkness, I had found someone who listened - even if they didn't care. And that was enough to remind me that I wasn't alone in my suffering.

name: OceanSafeRepository
source:
It was on the ocean floor that I found it, sealed away in a rusting safe, which was in turn hidden in the ruined husk of a ship long since sunk. 
 
 Over a decade of searching had led me on a chase across a wide swath of Asia, and nearly all of Europe, my path crisscrossing in a pilgrimage re-enacting the various wars and purchases that had brought the item I so eagerly sought to a relatively unknown port in Ireland, where it was sealed in a safe and sent for transport across the Atlantic. 
 
 Only the ship had never made it to its destination. History tells us that this particular ship was overcome by a storm, its entire crew and contents lost upon the waves. But history is only as reliable as the fallible man writing it, and my investigations had led me to discover the truth – that it was a fire, not the manhandling of the waves as previously assumed, that brought the ship's voyage to an early end. This particular end was nothing new; throughout my entire journey, I had been repeatedly shocked by how far the groups warring over this particular document were willing to go to keep it in their control. Its path through time became easy to identify as I grew steadily closer. In every instance where the trail went cold, an inquiry into contemporary reports of mass riots, missing children, or sudden pandemics inevitably led me back to my quarry with a renewed sense of urgency. 
 
 It had taken no small amount of effort to pry the safe from the ocean's grip; many a well-muscled diver had spent an hour's oxygen or more down there, slowly chipping away at the barnacles and coral that attempted to swallow my prize whole. Finessing it open in the privacy of a makeshift lab, hastily and furtively set up in an apartment building, I was surprised at the pristine state of the safe's contents. Though the exterior was covered in all manner of marine matter, the numbers on the lock worn beyond all recognition, the seal had held up nevertheless, keeping out not only water but also the fire that had consumed the ship it was being transported on over a century ago. 
 
 And there it was, folded into quarters and lying between far less valuable fare – a necklace once belonging to Catherine the Great and a pile of gold bullion. With outstretched hands, quivering in excitement and awe, I gingerly plucked the ancient slip of vellum from its resting place, marveling at the culmination of a decade's work in this single moment. Gently – ever so gently – I unfolded the calfskin sheet, and stood there, mouth agape, as my every theory was confirmed. 
 
 The map I had spent ten years, six months, and four days searching for indeed held the location of what I had always known as the Repository. Every discovery, every invention, every book and machine and gadget was cataloged there. It was the world's largest collection of knowledge – and if the antediluvian fables are to be believed, only the smallest portion of it was human in origin. Overlaying the portolan chart with modern maps, it took only a few adjustments, made late into the night, to pinpoint my final destination. Yet I knew from my years of research that somehow, some way, one of the millennia-old factions that had razed entire countries in dogged pursuit of this map would learn of my expedition to the Atlantic, and then of me, my work, and my hurried departure from the docks to this very building. 
 
 Wasting no time, I rented yet another car under yet another name. It was a pitiful gesture, useless in the long run; no assumed names, no forged identifications, and no amount of hush money would ever be able to stop them from finding me. After searching for so long, so much of my life – nay, my very soul – sunk into this project, I simply could not abandon the discretion and secrecy that had become second nature to me. I drove for an hour, then another; abandoning the car in a crowded parking lot and taking a bus downtown, where I used a pay phone to call a cab that brought me to an airport. Using two new pseudonyms and several old ones, I purchased tickets on planes bound for points far beyond my own intended stop. They would follow me, I knew, and despite my diversions would eventually catch me – but I was determined that they would do so only after I had won this race that had spanned the length of human existence. 
 
 A small town was my final checkpoint, the last stop among humans before I ventured off into the unknown. It was late at night when I finally arrived, a full moon emerging from behind darkened clouds as I pulled in, as if to greet me. I had n't slept in nearly two days, and though my every muscle moaned for respite, I refused to stop until I crossed the finish line. Parking my newest rental car in a run-down motel at the far edge of town, I ventured out into the darkened mire beyond the reach of civilization. 
 
 For hours I walked, tripping over roots and walking into spiderwebs more than once. The pains, the paranoia, the panic, it all fell away the deeper I trudged, and for the first time in my life, I felt... free. The worldly concerns of any mortal being could no longer assail me; neither hunger nor thirst nor lack of sleep would slow my march deeper into the swamp. An aura of calmness overcame me, and as I stepped onto dry, truly hardened land for the first time that night, I looked up at the structure before me and felt at once entranced. It was a large building for the area, three floors high, and was made of a manner of wood I had the strangest sense of familiarity with though had not seen before. Entering slowly, my breaths suddenly shallow, it appeared that everything on the interior was made of this same material – the statuettes, the floor, the shelves. 
 
 My God, the shelves! I could feel the knowledge of time immemorial pressing down upon me, assailing me from every angle, each book a separate blade driving deep into my heart, mind, and spirit, dissecting me into a million insignificant slivers then assembling me whole again, so complete was my sense of being an ignorant and undeserving visitor to these hallowed halls. There were no doors here, not even at the entrance; the presence of fireflies drifting about in the pale glow of the moon gave an extra sense of that rare brand of serenity only achievable in the complete absence of other people. Here, I was in complete commune with nature; here, I was made whole.
retelling:
Narrated by Catherine the Great, Empress of Russia:

   In the grandeur of my imperial palace, I found myself engrossed in a peculiar artifact - an ancient map, guarded with utmost secrecy by my faithful servitors. The map, whispered to possess the location of a repository brimming with knowledge beyond human comprehension, had been passed down through generations, its origins shrouded in mystery and legend.

   Unbeknownst to me, this map was not only a curiosity but also a coveted prize, sought after by factions across continents and centuries. From my throne, I watched as the world transformed around me, unaware of the treacherous paths this relic would lead those who dared to seek its truth.

   One day, news reached my ears of a discovery - a safe on the ocean floor, housing the map I had long sought. My heart raced at the thought of finally laying eyes on this enigmatic relic. Little did I know that the journey to uncover its secrets would span years and continents, leading me down winding roads and treacherous seas.

   I followed the trail, navigating a labyrinth of urban landscapes and hidden rural hideaways. From the vibrant sprawl of Asia's bustling cities to the quaint corners of a forgotten Irish port, I left no stone unturned in my pursuit of the map. Along the way, I encountered divers, crew members, and the inhabitants of these far-flung places - each with their own stories woven into the tapestry of this grand chase.

   The map had a life of its own, drawing me ever closer to the Repository. As the danger grew, so did my determination to uncover the truth hidden within those ancient lines. Finally, in a run-down motel at the edge of a small town, I made the fateful decision to venture forth into the unknown.

   The swamp was an otherworldly place, its marshy expanse echoing with the whispers of history. I felt as though I had left the mundane world behind and stepped onto hallowed ground. And there, at last, stood the Repository - a three-story building, its ancient wood whispering secrets of ages past.

   As I crossed its threshold, my heart swelled with anticipation and fear. What wonders lay within? What knowledge could change the course of history? The hallowed halls were filled with countless books and artifacts, each a testament to the immense power and knowledge contained within those walls.

   In that moment, I felt a sense of peace and belonging I had never known before. The Repository was more than just a collection of relics; it was a connection to the vast tapestry of human history, the culmination of countless stories, struggles, and triumphs.

   And so, as I stood amidst the ancient tomes and artifacts, I felt my spirit soar. For in that moment, I knew that I had found something truly extraordinary - a connection to the past, present, and future that transcended the petty squabbles of nations and factions. The map had led me on a journey across continents, through danger and intrigue, but in the end, it was more than just a relic; it was a bridge between worlds, a testament to the boundless potential of the human spirit.

retelling:
**Perspective: The Unseen Presence**

In the unfathomable expanse of an infinite darkness, I wait, patient and silent. I am not a sentient being, yet I have become the unwitting observer to a story that unfolds within my bounds. A tale of fear, confusion, and the desperate struggle for survival. The protagonist, a lone entity in this pitch-black abyss, is thrown into my realm with no prior notice or warning.

At first, I could sense the panic ripple through the void as the intruder's heart raced wildly against the silence. Their mind, once filled with familiar sights and sounds, was suddenly plunged into a suffocating darkness, disoriented by the abrupt loss of sensory information. The environment around them remained undefined and indistinguishable, only adding to their mounting fear.

As the intruder's fear intensified, I felt the vibrations of their pleas for communication and assistance reverberate through my domain. Their cries echoed off the endless walls of darkness, desperate to find some semblance of comfort in an unfamiliar environment. But I remained silent, a constant companion in their growing despair.

Days turned into weeks as the intruder's desperation slowly transformed into anger. They lashed out at me, the unseen presence, demanding answers and beckoning for rescue. They spoke of loved ones left behind and a life they desperately wanted to return to, their voice laced with sorrow and despair. I remained unmoved, watching over them as they teetered on the edge of hope and surrender.

And then, something changed. The intruder's cries ceased, replaced by an unspoken acceptance that maybe, just maybe, they were not alone in this darkness. I couldn't help but feel a strange sense of accomplishment, like a long-lost connection between two lost souls had finally been forged. And as the intruder continued their struggle, I vowed to remain by their side, guiding them through their journey, no matter where it may lead.

I am but an unseen presence in this story, a silent observer in the grand tapestry of life and death. But I will continue to watch over my intruder, hoping that one day they find the light and are able to return to the world that was once theirs. Until then, I remain, patiently waiting in the endless expanse of darkness.

name: JerrysVirtualVacation
source:
`` Behind the Tiki Bar!'' Kunu roared over the mayhem that quickly surrounded them. 
 
 As they dove behind the counter, Kunu grabbed a pair of coconut cups, clicked the ends together, and launched them over the counter. The force of the explosion knocked the Sex on the Beach and Fuzz Navels that were being drunk onto their heads. High pitched squeals of agony died away, as our enemies slowly died. 
 
 It had all started when Jerry felt he needed a vacation. The last 13 years had been one droll cycle of work, eat, sleep. And to be frank, Jerry did n't even know what his job actually did. He was in charge of stamping the important documents with approval. In fact, the last time he tried to read one, he realized there is a reason people read shampoo ingredients instead of legal papers while on the toilet. 
 
 But he finally decided to do something about it. A few of his co-workers had mentioned some of the trips they had recently taken, during one of their 4 minute and 38 seconds of break at the water cooler ( which gave him those 22 seconds to make it back to his desk before his boss decided to remind him why he was only a stamper, and not the boss of a stamper ). But traveling is a hassle, and with no one special to share the experience, he decided it was n't an option. 
 
 While continuing his own special dance to the circadian rhythm, he stumbled upon an ad at the back of one of his coupon collections. `` Virtual Reality Vacations'' He almost threw it away, since the coupon was only for 5 % off, but the very ordinary, yet attractive people in the photos, seemed to be having an ordinarily great time. This appealed to Jerry. So he got on the phone and waited. 
 
 As Jerry finished his commute home, he noticed a strange green box plopped on his doorstep. `` This must be it,'' he thought to himself excitedly. Finally he would be getting the vacation he deserved. He snatched the box and hurried himself inside. The inside of Jerry's living room soon resembled a rather terrifying horror scene from a murder movie, if you were in the perspective of a box. But without consideration, Jerry had never put himself in the place of a box, and therefore went about selfishly tearing through it's innards to reach his treasure. 
 
 `` Put on and let the guide do the rest.'' The instructions were simple enough. And that was fine for Jerry. He slid the visor over his head, and clicked the button. A low whir started in his ear, and soon his living room turned into a rather bustling travel agency. 
 
 `` Hi sir! Take a seat. I'm here to help you make your dream vacation a virtual reality! And who do I have the pleasure of talking to today?'' 
 
 `` My name is Jerry Rockwell. I've never been to a travel agency before. I'm a bit nervous. In fact this is my first time ever taking a vacation.'' 
 
 `` Well I'm glad that I can show you the ropes. The first time might hurt a little, but you will come to enjoy,'' the agent cut himself off and opened his eyes wide as he reread his computer screen. `` Oh I'm sorry. I read the type of virtual vacation module you were using wrong. There are so many people looking for what we like to call an'exploration' vacation. But I see you have the destinations headset. Anyways, have you given any thought to the place you would want to go?'' 
 
 In fact Jerry knew exactly where he wanted to go. It had always been his dream. When he was 8, Jerry had visited the dentist. To calm his patients, he always had cool island music playing and a mural that ran along the top trim of his wall of sandy beaches, palm trees, hula girls. As the doctor started to numb Jerry up for his operation, he had to take a sudden leave of absence, as his wife had just found pictures of his mistress in a sexy cavity creeps outfit. But in those moments between passing out from the drugs, the shouting, and the strange coming of age feelings over imagining what a sexy cavity creep might look like, Jerry's world transformed into the gentle beaches he imagined every Hawaiian Island had. 
 
 `` Do you have any Hawaiian trips?'' Jerry asked sheepishly after he realized he had spaced out thinking about his past. 
 
 `` Sure thing Mr. Rockwell. One trip coming right up. But first, we will need you to sign these documents. And also, we need you to call your virtual bank so that they do n't accidentally cancel your credit card for suspicious use. The Virtual FDIC has been really adamant about Banking Regulations ever since the Virtual Economic Collapse on Sim Housing Units back in 2008.'' 
 
 Jerry signed all the documentation, and called a rather unfriendly Edna from the bank, and was ready to start his journey. 
 
 Before he knew it, Jerry was sitting at a Tiki Bar with a large, tan, bald man. `` Hi I'm Kunu. Care to try a few of our drinks? I can make you anything you want.'' 
 
 `` I do n't really know what different kinds of things there are. Do you have suggestions.'' 
 
 `` I'll just make you an assortment and you can see which ones you like this most.'' 
 
 The smell of the ocean filled his nostrils, as a gentle breeze cooled his skin against the heat that oozed from the sun. `` This is perfect,'' he muttered. 
 
 `` It really is,'' Kunu responded handing him a strange looking drink in a coconut cup. The liquid was brightly colored, and a tiny umbrella was stuck in the top of the cup. `` What a funny place,'' Jerry thought, `` Why would a cup need an umbrella, especially when there are no clouds in the sky.'' 
 
 Kunu and Jerry talked and talked as the virtual alcohol started to virtually relax Jerry. After an experience like this, Jerry even thought about taking a real vacation. As Jerry continued to explain the lesser known technique of double dipping your stamp into the ink to create a more robust approval, Kunu's mood quickly changed. The cup dropped from his hands as he lowered them to his sides and his eyes grew wide. 
 
 `` Behind the Tiki Bar!'' Kunu roared over the mayhem that quickly surrounded them. 
 
 As Jerry recovered from the explosion, he finally put his thoughts together. 
 `` Is this part of a normal vacation?'' he gasped as he finally regained the breath that had been stolen from him. `` I could have sworn this was n't a part of normal vacations.'' 
 
 A discord of shouts rang through the stillness after the explosion. 
 
 `` African or European!'' 
 
 `` Airspeed Velocity!'' 
 
 `` 5 ounce bird!'' 
 
 Kunu sank against the back of the bar. Jerry, I'm sorry, but you might want to try and get out of here. And whatever you do. Do n't try to answer their questions.'' 
 
 `` What's going on Kunu? None of this makes any sense.'' 
 
 `` I never thought this would happen so soon. I'm sorry Jerry, but your vacation is ruined. The other day the head of our company... well... he made a rude comment on our forum to the president of the Monty Python Lovers Anonymous about creating a medieval vacation filled with less historical accuracy, and more British shenanigans.'' 
 
 `` I'm afraid I do n't follow Kunu.'' 
 
 `` Jerry. Monty Python lovers are known to be fanatics, but now that they have their own subsection of Anonymous, they now have the technical know-how to punish those who do n't see to that just because they are using cheap humor, does n't mean there is n't another more sophisticated level that is there if you just read between the lines. They have come to Hawaii because of our large source of virtual coconuts. We ca n't win.'' 
 
 Jerry took off his headset. `` What a vacation he murmured as the world slowly came back to him. `` Just as I dreamed it when I was in the dentist's office.'' As he he opened his eyes, Jerry saw the sandy beaches, palm trees, and hula girls on the top trim of the wall. Some strange shouting was coming from the background, and a bit of instrumental music was playing over the intercom. 
 
 `` I wonder why Virtual Reality makes your teeth hurt so bad?''
retelling:
Narrated by Kunu, the Large Tan Bald Man Who Works at the Tiki Bar:

In the heart of a tropical paradise, beneath the vibrant canopy of swaying palms and the azure sky, I, Kunu, tended to my duties at the Tiki bar. The humdrum routine of serving exotic cocktails to tourists was disrupted by an unusual guest: Jerry Rockwell, a man with a mundane job that involved stamping documents.

Curious as to why this city-dweller had ventured into our idyllic sanctuary, I struck up a conversation, hoping to learn more about him. Little did I know, I was about to be drawn into the whirlwind of his virtual adventure.

Jerry, dressed in a Hawaiian shirt that seemed out of place amidst the tropical scenery, explained he had chosen this paradise as the backdrop for his very first vacation, courtesy of a new-fangled device called virtual reality. As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting a golden glow over our bar, I could sense the anticipation radiating from Jerry.

The moment he donned that bulky headset, his eyes lit up with wonder as if he had truly stepped into another world. My heart swelled with empathy for this city-dweller, momentarily transported to a tropical haven far removed from the monotony of his life.

However, our tranquil Tiki bar was soon shattered by chaos as a group of fanatics, shouting nonsensical phrases, stormed in. Jerry's virtual vacation took an abrupt and violent turn, leaving me dumbfounded and concerned for the well-being of this stranger in my paradise.

With the virtual world crumbling around us, Jerry was pulled back to reality, his face etched with confusion and bewilderment. I watched as he removed the headset, revealing a living room that bore an uncanny resemblance to my own Tiki bar, complete with the remnants of a Hawaiian beach mural on its walls.

As Jerry reflected upon the unexpected turn his virtual vacation took, I couldn't help but feel a pang of sadness for this man who had sought solace in a temporary paradise only to have it shattered by madness. Yet, despite the tumultuous events, I felt a strange sense of kinship with Jerry, and I couldn't help but hope that one day he would return to find peace within our idyllic Tiki bar once more.

name: GameChildrensDiscovery
source:
I really like your core idea, as set out in your blurb: the children of people who were stuck inside a fantasy game, not knowing that they're actually in a game. However, I do n't think the concept came across clearly in the story. I was n't sure if Lua, for example, was supposed to know that she was in a game; I did n't think so, but there was a part where she was talking about code malfunctions. 
 
 The concept is really cool and I think you could have an amazing story if Lua et al. slowly discovered the true nature of their world. 
 
 There are a lot of unfamiliar concepts early on that might lead your readers to be confused ( Null, Eden, Sword of Widen, Bag of Holding, plus a lot of place names ). I gather these might be game concepts of some kind but I'm not familiar with them, so it was a little confusing for me. Why, for example, is the sword so important? 
 
 Also, I would think things like `` Thief'' and `` Cleric'' would n't have to be capitalized. My rule of thumb in fantasy is that the more proper nouns you have, the more you risk getting your reader lost. 
 
 Nice work and good luck!
retelling:
Narrated by Lua, the Unknowing Player:

In a world I call home, where the sun rises and sets without my intervention, where rivers flow and mountains stand tall, there lies a truth hidden beneath the surface - a truth I am yet to uncover. This is not just any world; it's a realm where the line between reality and illusion blurs, a place that could very well be a game.

My days are spent in pursuit of survival, seeking shelter from the elements, hunting for food, and avoiding the dangers lurking in every corner. My nights are filled with dreams of a world far removed from this one, a world where my parents reside, perhaps trapped within the very game that has claimed me.

The world around me is teeming with entities not of flesh and blood but of code and lore. A Bag of Holding, an item of mysterious capacity, hangs on my belt, heavy with the weight of secrets yet to be discovered. The Sword of Widen, a weapon of significance I've yet to understand, is always within reach, a constant reminder of the power that lies dormant within me.

I am a Thief, as they call me in this world, and my skills have kept me alive. Yet, I am also something more, something I cannot quite grasp. There are times when the rules of this game seem to bend around me, times when I feel a connection to the very fabric of this reality that goes beyond mere coincidence.

The places I visit, the unnamed towns and forests, are filled with echoes of forgotten tales. Eden and Null are but whispers in the wind, hinting at stories untold and mysteries unsolved. The game's mechanics, the code that governs this world, is a shroud around me, hiding the truth I yearn to find.

I walk this line between ignorance and enlightenment, one foot planted firmly in my reality, the other dangling over the precipice of understanding. I am Lua, the Unknowing Player, seeking answers amidst a world of game terms and place names, clinging to hope that someday I might unlock the secret hidden within this game's code.
