name: DeathDealChoice
source:
`` Do you do this for everyone?'' I asked, face pale, eyes not leaving the image frozen in the windshield. 
 
 `` No,'' the figure perched like a black-winged vulture on the hood admitted, words clearly audible despite the intervening wall of glass between us. `` Only in... special cases.'' 
 
 `` And what are the terms?'' It was queer, that I did not find myself doubting the hunched mass of black cloth and white bone. Is that what madness was like? Where the visions assailed you and each new one only increased your confidence in their reality? Surely I was in the grasp of some lunatic delusion, but I listened anyway, and I believed every word as truth. 
 
 `` You can die. Or you can reach out from where you sit and touch any other human being and they will die in your place. You can not affect the world in any other way and when I depart -- with you or with another -- no one who remains behind will have any memory of what has transpired.'' 
 
 `` What am I even dying of?'' 
 
 `` Sudden, massive heart attack,'' Death said, his shoulders shrugging a little in apology. `` You spend too much time worrying at work, Henry. It is bad for your health.'' 
 
 To one side of the car, a sheer wall of stone rose as the mountain's face climbed up into the evening mist. On the other side, the yawning drop down across the mountain's face, coated with a deceptively serene blanket of trees. 
 
 `` So you just come down here to make the devil's deal?'' I was fighting back tears now. 
 
 Beside me, Marelene had her purse in her lap and she was fishing for something in it; probably her gum. She'd been drinking coffee to try and stay awake, but she hated the taste and was always quick to try and overpower it with sweets after finishing her cup. In the back seat, George had his nose almost pressed against the screen of his phone, either texting one of his friends back home or playing a game of some sort; the reception was too bad out here for him to be browsing the internet. The twins were napping next to him, their hands clasped as they always did when the pair were relaxed. 
 
 `` Most people would be thankful for the chance.'' He -- *it* -- seemed a little hurt when it spoke. `` The chance to save at least something.'' 
 
 And in my hand, the steering wheel.
retelling:
**Narrative Perspective: Marelene**

   As I sat in the passenger seat of Henry's car, my eyes fixated on the winding mountain road ahead. The sun was setting, casting long shadows over the steep cliff faces, and the car swayed precariously with each twist and turn. George was engrossed in his phone, oblivious to the world outside, while the twins slumbered peacefully in the back seat.

   Suddenly, a figure appeared on the hood of the car. It looked like Death itself, its features indistinct yet undeniably eerie. I felt my heart leap into my throat as Henry pulled over, the car's tires screeching against the asphalt.

   "Henry?" I asked, my voice trembling. He didn't respond, his eyes locked on the figure before us. Death stepped off the hood, moving with an unsettling grace, and approached the car. It extended a hand to Henry, offering him a choice.

   I couldn't hear what was being said, but I saw Henry's face contort in confusion and fear. The figure seemed disappointed, its eyes flicking toward me before turning back to Henry. It was then that I realized the gravity of the situation – we were all in danger.

   In the silence that followed, I gripped the door handle tightly, my mind racing with thoughts. What was happening? Why had Death come for us? And why did it seem displeased with Henry's response? As the car remained still, I braced myself for whatever was to come next, my heart pounding in my chest.

name: alphaCentauriTypo
source:
Strapped In 
 
 It was a typo. It must have been a typo. Some engineer rushing to meet deadlines transposed a 7 and an 8. 
 
 We emerged from our slumber on schedule on May 26th, 2178. We had made it to Alpha Centauri. We were orbiting around a small planetoid in the system. Everything worked perfectly. Life support was at normal levels. We were the first astronauts to venture outside the solar system. We were the first of hopefully many missions to the great beyond. This was the first mission of the newly rebuilt space program called simply WASP ( or World Aeronautics and Space Program ). After the fallout from the War of the Great Powers, the world came together as one to rebuild. It had been 100 years since the truce and the world was at peace. The masses from the great leaders down to the janitors were well fed and educated and otherwise taken care of. No one went without but crowd control was becoming an issue. 12 billion people on one blue rock and the numbers were exploding. With everybody getting healthier, there was new breeding stock. Maternal and Infant mortality was near zero even in what were once considered third world countries. 
 
 Population control was talked about. However, the great leaders could n't agree on a limit. And eugenics practices were one of the instigators of the War. So the space program was reintroduced. We would build FTL engines that would get us to Earth-like planets. WASP was built from the ground up. We had data from the space agencies of old. We put together all the scraps we could find. Our ship was basically a tin can patched together with other tin cans with a hastily built computer in it. 
 
 I stress hastily built. We emerged from our slumber on schedule on May 26th, 2178. However, the cryo-chamber was set to open on May 26th, 2187. I could n't blame anybody really. The mission was put together in all of five years from first mention til now. I could practically see the programmer working late into the night. I can feel his heart racing at the thought of what his supervisor would say if he did n't finish the code. But I can also feel his eyes start to droop as he nears completion. He just needs to input the dates now. 7 and 8 are *so* close on the keyboard... 
 
 My thoughts are interrupted by a scream from my commanding officer. All control lost. Just two days in the chamber has driven him past the point of rational thought. There are red smears on the transparent casing of the chamber where he has punched and kicked at the walls. His hands and feet broken into unrecognizable pulps. It is no use. The casing is made of a hardened carbon nanofiber. The thought was to make a chamber capable of withstanding extreme environment changes. My CO is now banging his head on the walls. He will soon be dead if his hands and feet are any indication. 
 
 I assume rational thought will leave me at some point as well. Maybe when my body starts to eat itself from starvation? Maybe when dehydration sets in? I do not know. I only know it has been two days because of my HUD. It ticks off every second. I can pull up anything about the ship that I want. I can even pilot it from here. However, it will take another six months to get back home. Also, the chambers can only be reset once they have been opened. 
 
 In an hour or so, my CO is dead or near dead. I pull up communications and send out a communique to Earth. They wo n't receive it for four or so years. However, they deserve to know what happened. In as calm a voice as I can manage, I detail our situation. 
 
 It's not long after that dehydration comes along. I have a massive headache. I ca n't bring myself to self-mutilation. Does that make me a coward? My stomach is one big cramp. Another day or two, I ca n't move my arms or legs because they hurt and I have no energy to move them. I can no longer support my weight so I slump down in the chamber. I want to cry but I have no tears. Now, if I wanted to punch and kick at the chamber, I would n't be able to. A day or so, unconsciousness follows me. I never wake again. I'm still strapped in.
retelling:
Character: **The Commanding Officer (CO)**

   In the cold, sterile confines of our hastily assembled tin can, floating aimlessly in the vast expanse of the Alpha Centauri System, I found myself at the helm of a mission that should have been an historic triumph for mankind but instead became a tragic tale of human error and hubris.

I stood tall, a symbol of discipline and leadership, as I addressed my crew before we embarked on this journey to terraform a new world for our rapidly growing population back on Earth. Little did I know that the seed of destruction had already been sown, hidden in the intricate web of code that controlled the very life support system of our vessel.

On that fateful day of May 26th, 2178, my crew and I awoke from our cryo-sleep to find ourselves stranded in space for an unimaginable amount of time. The error was so simple, so insidious - a single typographical mistake that had catastrophic consequences. It struck me then that the human spirit, despite its incredible capacity for innovation and exploration, could also be its own worst enemy.

As the days turned into weeks, the situation aboard our vessel deteriorated rapidly. Rations dwindled, and the once-vibrant faces of my crew began to pale and fade. My heart ached with every crippling blow that threatened their lives. I tried to maintain order, to keep hope alive, but as each day passed, I felt the weight of my responsibilities crushing me like the cold vacuum of space.

In my darkest hour, I succumbed to despair. The strain of leading this doomed expedition took its toll on my sanity, and I found myself unable to bear the burden any longer. In a moment of madness, I turned on the communication system and sent a message back to Earth - a message that would take four long years to reach their intended destination. I told them of our plight, of the horror that had befallen us, and begged for forgiveness and mercy.

But there was no answer, only silence. The cold, unfeeling void that surrounded me seemed to swallow up my cries for help, leaving me alone with my guilt and regret. I could see the hopelessness in the eyes of my crew - the realization that their lives would end here, far from home and without a hero's welcome.

In the end, it was not the cruel cosmos or our own mistakes that claimed us, but the relentless march of time. One by one, my crew fell to starvation and dehydration, until there was only I, left to bear witness to our tragic fate. And so, in this desolate corner of the universe, I awaited my own end - a fittingly lonely epilogue to a story of ambition and folly.

As I drift away into the cold embrace of eternity, I cannot help but wonder if there is some small chance that our sacrifice was not in vain. Perhaps the people of Earth will learn from our mistakes and strive for greater understanding and caution in their pursuit of the stars. And if even a single life is spared because of our story, then perhaps my service - and the lives of those I loved so dearly - will have had some meaning after all.

name: SoulWindowsCycle
source:
The windows to his soul were pried open wide 
 Stuck on death, chaos, confusion, fear, 
 Watching as the surrounding life and all he held dear 
 Would do nothing but continually steer 
 Him to a cycle of time that would not step aside. 
 
 Countless doors slamming into his face 
 As each blink recalls yet another key thrown 
 Into drowning silence, the locked and unknown 
 Now common, collected, forever sown 
 By a mind running a circular race. 
 
 A gentle caress does nothing to repair 
 Such battered hinges, broken frames, 
 Piled atop windowless sills etched with names 
 Of the lasting moments, those whose aims 
 Are to lock him away, with just enough air.
retelling:
Narrator: The silent observer, a detached entity confined within the labyrinth of the protagonist's mind, bearing witness to his tormented existence.

   In the vast expanse of time and space, there exists an eternal cycle, a circular race that entraps one soul - Him. This soul is trapped in a world that pulses with death, chaos, confusion, fear; a realm where his emotions and experiences are the landscape.

   From my vantage point, I see the countless doors slamming shut upon him, each slam echoing through the void, resonating with the rhythm of despair. The mind that houses him is in constant motion, running in circles like a ship lost at sea, seeking solace it cannot find.

   His attempts at escaping this maze are as futile as a bird attempting to break free from its cage. He reaches out for gentle caresses, but they offer only temporary relief before being swept away by the tide of fear and chaos once more.

   Beyond the veil of his mind, I sense a hostile reality that seems indifferent to his suffering. The external world is locked and unknown, symbolized by the windowless sills and just enough air to keep him alive but never truly free.

   Yet, amidst all this suffering, there remains a spark - a flicker of life. A testament to his resilience, a beacon in the darkness that speaks volumes about his indomitable spirit.

   Despite my role as an observer, I cannot help but feel a strange connection with him. For every door that slams shut, I am reminded of the unyielding nature of our existence. And for every circle he runs, I see a reminder of our shared human struggle against adversity.

   In the end, I remain here, observing, bearing witness to his plight. Will I ever understand his pain? Perhaps not. But perhaps it is enough for me to simply bear witness, to offer my silent support through the countless doors that slam shut upon him.

name: MarianaTrenchImmortal
source:
I was suffocating. No, not suffocating. I was drowning. 
 
 Water rushed into my mouth and down my throat, filling my stomach and lungs, as I screamed, yelled and cried out. Around me there was nothing but crushing blackness, so dark that that I could feel it like a physical weight trying to break me. It was pushing in on my limbs and head until it felt like I was going to explode. But darkness could n't do that, darkness had no physical weight, it must have been the water I was clearly submerged in. I thrashed in panic at the thought and started to yell again, only to start gagging as more water rushed in. Something was attached to my foot, clearly keeping me weighed down. I should have been dead by now. 
 
 I was bitterly cold, in a way that made the marrow in my bones ache. It was the kind of cold that caused you to lose body parts. It was the kind of cold that killed. I had already started to shiver so violently that my limbs had started to twitch. I tried to move, but chain kept me anchored and the current at my back kept bringing a constant steam of cold pressing against my body. 
 
 Dimly, I realised I had been conscious, under water for several minutes now and I was still alive. The burning need to breathe was getting worse with every second, and panic was starting to bubble under my skin, but I was somehow still conscious and alive. I was in too much pain not to be. 
 
 Something brushed against my right wrist and I twisted in panic. My mind raced, imagining a multitude of gruesome sea creatures that could be circling around me, and I was completely blind to what they were in this blackness. My body jolted and I thrashed around some more, only for whatever it was to brush against me again. Instinctively I grabbed it, and braced myself for the feeling of cold scales. I was surprised when, instead, I grabbed onto cold plastic. I pulled it in close and felt it with two hands. It was a plastic cylander, with a round face, and what felt like strips of fabric hanging from it. I fumbled it almost urgently in my hands, trying to figure out what it was, and gave a cry of alarm when a light suddenly flared to life. 
 
 It took a moment for my eyes to focus enough in the water, to make sense of what I was holding. It was a torch. I was holding a torch! A quick examination revealed the strips of fabric were actually a harness to attach it to my head. I shone the light in a circle around me, trying to make out what I could of my surroundings, but there was nothing. Two feet below me was the ocean floor, to my left nothing but water, and to my right was a sheer wall of rock. I wasted no time in strapping the torch to my head and then looked down. 
 
 A length of chain circled my ankle and stretched off into the water below me, ending where it appeared to be attached to a mass of what looked like lead weights. I gripped onto the chain and used it to pull me downwards, until I was able to grab one of the weights. Whilst I did n't feel like I was about to float upwards, the water made it hard to control where my body went. 
 
 It was n't until I was directly above the weights that I noticed the piece of paper. It was trapped beneath the top weight, and had been laminated. I reached out for it eagerly, and was relieved to see that it had been written in large, bold letters. It would be easy to read despite the blurriness caused by the water. 
 
 *'' You're now immortal. Welcome to the bottom of the Marianna Trench. This is your first test. `` * 
 
 My heart lurched as I scrambled to make sense of what I had just read. My heart hammered faster and faster as I considered the words Immortal, and Marianna Trench. What the hell had happened to me? 
 
 I could n't deny that I was immortal. I had been under water for nigh on fifteen minutes now, and even though I could feel the need to breath like an agonising inferno in my chest, I was still alive, still concious. I could n't die. As for the Marianna Trench, I had no way to know if it was true, but I had no reason not to believe it. Even that leant credence to my apparent new found immortality. The pressure at this depth should have been enough, alone, to kill me. And yet here I was. 
 
 How had I gotten here? 
 
 I tried hard to think of the last thing I remembered. Images flashed through my mind, fleeting and indistinct. There was nothing substantial there for me to grab onto as I tried to force something, anything to click into place. Suddenly red lips and dark skin flashed before me, so vibrant I could almost see them floating before me. I scrambled for it in my mind and held on. Flawless, ebony skin and glittering eyes. Red, red lips peeled back in a terrifying smile to reveal teeth too white, too perfect to be real. I could feel the memory slipping, and I strained with every ounce of mental fortitude I possed to hold onto it. She formed in my mind. A perfectly tailored suit, long dark hair pulled back in a pony tail. I could feel her breath against my ear, and hear the low voice, `` Do you want to live forever?'' 
 
 A shiver wracked my body and my concentration slipped, and the memory went with it. I thought hard, but all I could remember was the image of her, and her crimson lips. So very, very red. And there it was, the edge of another memory washed in red. As I pulled it towards me every one of my senses filled with red. I could taste and smell it's coppery tang, feel its slickness on my hands and face, hear it in the screams of... I let the memory go, my heart pounding anew. No, not a memory. That was a nightmare. 
 
 *This is your first test. * 
 
 I had no idea what it meant. I did n't have time to figure it out. I had to get to the surface of wherever I had been dropped and make it back to land. The chain slipped over my foot easily enough with a bit of force, and my body began to float upwards. I quickly grabbed for the weights, using them to bring my feet to the ocean floor, and then I grabbed two from the pile to keep me weighted in place. 
 
 If my limited memory of Geography was serving me right, the northern tip of the Mariana Trench was off the south-eastern coast of Japan. With the rock wall to my right, following it should take me in that direction. I did n't give myself time to think about how they had gotten me this far across the world, or how far I would have to walk to get there. I tried not to remember that it was nearly two and a half thousand kilometers long. I just forced myself to move. I took slow, laborious steps, one after the other, ignoring the pain in my chest and the ache in my bones. I focused on the flurry of sand and mud as it floated around me, disturbed by my footsteps, and tried not to think about the deep sea creatures that might be watching my progress. 
 
 Ahead, a rock seemed to loom up in the shadows, directly in my path. It looked to be an equal height with myself and just as wide, and I moved towards the wall to avoid it. The rock followed my movements. I stopped as abruptly as I could and surveyed the rock that had clearly just moved back into my path. I took several slow steps forward until the light from my torch shone directly onto it. 
 
 Ebony skin. Red, red lips. 
 
 I swallowed back a scream that would not help me here. 
 
 I was not alone in the trench.
retelling:
Perspective: The Woman with Red Lips and Dark Skin

In the deep recesses of the Mariana Trench, a woman with red lips and dark skin awaited her target's arrival. Her eyes, gleaming like the precious stones found in the abyss, watched as the northern tip of Japan loomed in the distance. She was not alone; her companion, a monstrous creature resembling a rock, moved steadily towards their destination, its form taking shape under the absolute darkness.

The woman had been observing this trench for eons, biding her time until the perfect candidate emerged—a soul with the capacity to challenge destiny itself. The one who arrived now was different; he seemed both terrified and curious, a rare combination indeed. As she watched him fumble through his fragmented memories, she saw glimpses of their past, of a life lived beyond the trench's depths.

Intrigued, she let her thoughts drift back to that moment when they had crossed paths. She recalled the offer she made—immortality in exchange for obedience and service to her cause. The man had hesitated but eventually agreed, his eyes filled with hope and desperation. Now, as he struggled against the weights attached to his ankle, she could not help but feel a pang of nostalgia.

The woman knew that the journey towards the surface would be arduous for her charge. The trench was treacherous, its depths concealing dangers unimaginable by mere mortals. But as long as he remained faithful, she would guide him through the darkness, helping him navigate the twists and turns of the ocean floor.

As the man moved closer to Japan, the woman watched with a mixture of satisfaction and anticipation. The test was far from over, but she knew that her pawn had already proven his worth by surviving against all odds. With each step forward, he was one step closer to fulfilling their pact—and to unleashing chaos upon the world above.

name: JimmysPelletGunMishap
source:
“ Jimmy! ” Yelled Mrs. Cleemer, “ Jimmy, stop shooting in other people ’ s yards! ” 
 
 
 Jimmy looked over and realized that he couldn ’ t blow her off. He lowered the pellet rifle. He walked, his head hung low in defeat. Somewhere in the Davis ’ s yard was injured squirrel on its last legs that he would have to let go until his Mom was done chewing him out. Mrs. Cleemer with her peach colored blouse and white slacks stood disapprovingly with her arms crossed in front of her as her son reluctantly Marched to the back porch. 
 
 It was a beautiful clear day for shooting. This is what worried Mrs. Cleemer. 
 
 “ Jimmy, what have I told you? ” She asked with the same sickening air of superiority. 
 
 “ To stay in our yard. ” 
 
 “ That ’ s right Mister. ” She said turning up her nose, “ Now come on, I need you to take something to the new neighbor over on Enos Road. ” 
 
 “ Hmm? ” 
 
 Jimmy ’ s interest was piqued. Enos road had a lot of smaller critter to shoot, rabbit and squirrel. If he was being sent over there out of the immediate supervision of his Mother, then there would be a bit of hell to raise. 
 
 “ Just be careful, ” began Mrs. Cleemer before she was interrupted by her son, 
 
 “ They drive crazy out here, if not drunk. I know, I know, ” began the exasperated teenager, 
 
 “ No, not that, ” said Mrs. Cleemer, “ I hear that the new neighbors are very eccentric, just make sure you don ’ t do anything weird near their property and leave your gun. ” 
 
 “ Mom! ” 
 
 “ No, I ’ m not hearing it, ” began Mrs. Cleemer, “ give me this, ” 
 
 The pellet gun was roughly yanked out of Jimmy ’ s hands and reluctantly took the small carton of pellets out of his cargo shorts. 
 
 “ Now, ” said Mrs. Cleemer putting the pellet gun in the corner near the sliding glass door, “ Take this cake over to them, they live next to the Barbrady ’ s. ” 
 
 “ Okay, ” 
 
 “ And why don ’ t you say hi to Chelsea afterwards? ” 
 
 “ I ’ d rather shoot myself, ” 
 
 “ Jimmy! ” Shrieked his mother. 
 
 Jimmy took the opportunity to run faster to his bike, the cake in a bag clutched by his right hand. He immediately placed it in the basket and rode out. The clear, summer day had not yet graced the world with an unbearable amount of heat, allowing Jimmy to enjoy the trip. He was a bit angry he couldn ’ t shoot over on Enos this morning. 
 
 He brought himself to the house, a rather plain ranch style house with a gravel driveway, almost like every other house out here, and rung the doorbell. The door swung open and a beautiful, tall blonde women greeted him, 
 
 “ Hello, ” said the woman, “ You are our neighbor? ” 
 
 Jimmy ’ s mouth hung open. She was beautiful and the dress that hung loosely on her frame beautifully silhouetted that figure. Her thick, accent only added to the exotic appeal to Jimmy who suddenly felt his ‘ jimmies ’ being rustled. 
 
 “ I- I brought this over. My mom wanted to greet you to the neighborhood. ” 
 
 “ Oh, how sweet, ” said the woman as she grasped the bag. 
 
 “ I ’ m, I ’ m Jimmy. Jimmy Cleemer. ” 
 
 “ Come in Jimmy, ” said the woman with a smile, turning and walking into the house. She walked past the familiar living room directly into the kitchen, which Jimmy remembered eating in with Jason back when he still lived in the house. Jimmy didn ’ t notice any of the new additions or furniture, like the African Tribal masks or the strange ebony statues. He was too busy trying to stare a hole into the back of the woman ’ s dress, “ My name is Laura. ” 
 
 “ Nice to meet you Mrs. Laura, ” said Jimmy, trying his best to act polite but unable to resist wholeheartedly gawking at the woman. 
 
 “ I am from France, but I ’ ve spent some time abroad studying in culture in Africa. I wanted to move here to do a write up on my research in peace, but I ’ m sure you don ’ t want to hear about any of that, ” 
 
 Laura had placed the cake on the counter and grabbed a pitcher of what seemed to fruit juice from the refrigerator. She noticed Jimmy staring at her body and smiled. 
 
 “ Here, it ’ s a beautiful day, would have a glass with me? ” 
 
 “ Y-Yes, Ma ’ am. ” 
 
 Jimmy followed the woman out to the porch and took a seat at the table but noticed there were no glasses. Laura leaned in towards Jimmy and softly touched his face, causing him to blush. 
 
 “ Jimmy, you ’ re a handsome young boy. ” 
 
 Jimmy blushed harder, turning almost as red as the liquid in that pitcher Laura was holding. As she leaned closer, Jimmy ’ s eyes began to close. Surprisingly, instead of a soft pair of lips, Jimmy felt the hard glass of the pitcher hitting his teeth as the liquid was poured into his mouth. Some of it he reflexively spat out. Some went into his windpipe causing him to cough. The rest was poured over him. 
 
 “ Yes, you ’ ll do Jimmy, you ’ ll do. ” 
 
 Jimmy was coughing violently and felt sticky from the syrupy liquid. He stood up and stumbled back against the house. As he began to regain hold of himself he heard the buzzing. It wasn ’ t the normal buzzing of Cicadas and Katydids, it was a swarm. It came from all around him. 
 
 “ SHIT! ” 
 
 Jimmy looked down at his arm and there was a wasp. He jerked again as he felt something on his neck, and his back and his leg. All over, thousands of biting sensations began to cover him. He yelled out and Laura stood there enjoying the sight.
retelling:
**Narrative Perspective: The Injured Squirrel**

   From the rustling leaves overhead, I could sense a presence approaching. A boy named Jimmy, with his pellet rifle in hand, had entered my territory, the lush and bustling yard of Enos Road. The air was thick with anticipation; it wasn't long before the first shot rang out, echoing through the trees.

   I had no idea what this strange device was, but I knew it meant danger. I quickly scurried across the yard, trying to avoid his line of sight, only to find myself cornered near the Davis' house. The second shot found its mark; I felt a sharp pain as a pellet pierced my side.

   A scream echoed from within the Davis' house, but no one seemed to notice me lying there, injured and helpless. Jimmy had already moved on, his laughter ringing through the air as he continued his hunt.

   Time passed slowly. The sun grew higher in the sky, casting long shadows over the road that led back to the Cleemer's yard. A kind-faced woman, Mrs. Cleemer, arrived at the Davis' house with a box in her hands. I could hear her scolding Jimmy for his reckless actions.

   But the sound of my pain seemed to have fallen on deaf ears. The pellet rifle was taken away, but not before causing irreparable damage. I lay there, alone and forgotten, as the day grew long and the sun began to set.

   It wasn't until the following morning that I was found by a kind-hearted girl named Chelsea. She gently picked me up, her touch soothing my wounds. Despite my injuries, I couldn't help but feel a glimmer of hope. Perhaps this day wouldn't end in tragedy after all.

   And so, I tell you my tale, not as a mere squirrel, but as a symbol of the consequences of thoughtless actions and the resilience of life itself. The memory of that fateful day on Enos Road will forever remain etched in my mind, a reminder of a boy's carelessness and the power of second chances.

name: HumanSaviorRedemption
source:
“ Shame, ” I shouted as I turned in a circle. The eyes of the assembly were all on her in this moment. “ I am not the one who should be ashamed. ” My eyes seemed to bore into the three council members on the dais. “ You are the ones who could not see past your own importance to see the potential these humans have. They will be the ones to save us all. Not your mighty council or your all-important enclave. These humans that have been slaves will rise up and they will do what you have only dreamed about. I will gladly trade my life to save this human knowing that one day he may be the one to accomplish everything. ” 
 “ So be it. ” The words of the council wash over me as I lost consciousness. 
 5 years later….. 
 The men of the council watched from their cell as a statue went up in the courtyard. 
 The human I had saved that day whispered through the bars, “ She was the greatest of you all and we will remember. ” His crown winked in the sunlight as he walked away amidst the cheering of the finally free people of Earth.
retelling:
Perspective: The Human Slave Turned King

In the heart of an assembly hall, beneath the watchful eyes of three unnamed council members perched atop a lofty dais, I, a slave to the oppressive regime, stood shackled and trembling before my captors. The unnamed narrator, a figure of defiance and courage, spoke words that would forever change my destiny.

He declared that my worth was not in servitude but in potential, a gift overlooked by the blinded council members who had failed to recognize our true capabilities. With a heart as vast as the universe, he offered his life in exchange for mine, an offer the council accepted without hesitation.

Five long years later, I found myself crowned and standing before the same cold stone walls of the very prison that once held me captive. The council members, now prisoners themselves, looked up at me with expressions of bewilderment and anger, their eyes transfixed by a towering statue erected in my honor - a testament to the narrator's sacrifice and our newfound freedom.

I felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude towards this mysterious individual who had risked everything for someone as unworthy as me. The narrator's greatness was not confined to the pages of history, but resounded in every heart that yearned for justice and equality. I knew that our journey was far from over, and that the spirit of the narrator would continue to guide us towards a brighter future.

In the courtyard outside, the once oppressed people celebrated their newfound freedom, their laughter echoing through the air as they gathered around the statue of the narrator - a symbol of hope, unity, and the power of the human spirit. I joined them, feeling a sense of pride and determination surge through me, knowing that our liberation was just the beginning.

name: SaraWestonExperiment
source:
Sara Weston calmly walked up to the test bench. A crowd of men, most bespectacled and all adorned in crisp white lab coats, stood nearby; their hands, pens at the ready, poised above sheets of paper supported by clean clipboards. Sara tried to remain calm, she tried not to shrink away from the dozens of stern gazes cast her way. 
 
 On top of the test bench, there was a pan, dirtied from cooking; grease and oil sat in the pan, congealed. A small bit of water pooled in one corner. Across from the test bench, a sink sat; cleaning supplies and a bright yellow sponge sat next to the sink. The task was simple, to clean the pan, without incident. The test group before Sara had failed dramatically, somehow setting fire to the laboratory. 
 
 But, this failure would not follow Sara Weston. The woman was different, otherworldly even. She ’ d been discovered, one day, by the elite group of scientists as they went house to house, recruiting lab subjects; they were desperately attempting to cure the simpleminded clumsiness that appeared to be plaguing the denizens of the Earth. 
 
 It was then, as they moved on from a house suffering a rather tragic grease fire, to the humble abode of Sara Weston. Her house had seemed miraculously in one piece; her car in perfect working order. When they had rung the doorbell, they ’ d been surprised by Sara ’ s lack of commotion or accident as she ’ d opened the door, and easily let them inside. They had stared in wonder as they noticed a lack of fire marks, stains, or other such damages to her home. They ’ d instantly asked her join in their research, offering a hefty sum of money as incentive. Sara had agreed instantly, desperate for money and self-motivated to help human society in any way possible. 
 
 That was how Sara found herself, carefully picking up the pan, ringed by dozens of middle-aged men furiously writing notes. Several nodes and wires covered her body, recording data on her vitals every second. 
 
 Sara walked the pan over to the sink. In determination, she turned on the hot water and squeezed out some detergent into the pan and then onto the sponge. A steady stream of hot water fell into the sink, falling onto the dirty pan and down the drain. After an application of solid elbow grease, Sara easily cleaned the dirty pan. She placed the hunk of cast iron on the drying rack, and turned back to face the scientists. 
 
 A collective mutter of disbelief filled the room as the scientists looked up from their notes. A few of the clipboards were dropped, soft swears accompanied their descent. They were not dropped from surprise, but merely from a clumsiness that even the greatest scientists of the world were not immune to. They were amazed, there hadn ’ t been a fire. The first instance of a fireless experiment in over three years. The men were completely baffled, utterly amazed. 
 
 They ushered Sara out of the testing room, and began another test, and then another one after that. These men spent over half a year putting Sara Weston through all of their trials. She took out the garbage, washed the car, properly used a hose, stored food in the fridge, and many, many other activities. All the while, the scientists stared in amazement, recording every detail and discernible piece of data. 
 
 After this period of experiment, the men turned to their data. They fell upon the numbers and calculations like vultures, tearing into their science. With only the slight office fire, or spilt coffee on their keyboards or computers, they worked with an earnest. These men were the brightest minds the world had to offer, assembled by the governments of the world to create a cure for this uncanny clumsiness which seemed to permeate throughout the people, despite any sort of cultural or political barriers. 
 
 It was after years of research, of experimenting and data analysis, that the scientists finally had assembled an answer; a harrowing answer at that. Presented at a special conference, holding all of the world ’ s leaders, were the results of the scientists ’ years of efforts. It seemed to them that the denizens of the Earth, barring Sara Weston, suffered from a distinct mental disability. It was a flaw, a rewiring in their brains caused by a seemingly insignificant genetic flaw, which created a motor-cognitive failure. It was not that the denizens of the world were simply clumsy, they were genetically programmed to be accident prone. 
 
 There was a collective sigh of disappointment from the leaders of the world. The councilmen from China accidentally fell out of their chairs during the sigh, the president of the United States accidentally slapped himself in the face when he ’ d meant to grab his pen. 
 
 The scientists, the presenters, felt nothing but fear for the human race. They ’ d lost contact with Sara Weston, their key to the future, and hadn ’ t been able to contact her. Some speculated that her existence in their world had, in itself, been an accident; the ultimate act of clumsiness acted on by the universe itself. Whatever the reason, it seemed that Sara Weston no longer existed in this world, or if she did, then she was able to avoid the greatest governments in the world as they searched for her. 
 
 It was with a heavy heart that the leaders of the world revealed this news to their citizens, and of their inability to find a cure. There would have been pandemonium on the streets from the outrage of the citizens, but if had been any, it had been indistinguishable from the usual chaos of crashes, fires, accidents, and other chaos caused by simple clumsiness. 
 
 To the despair of the scientists, their work had been for naught, and the world continued to turn, filled with the accidental chaos which now, to them, seemed to be the work of nature, or of God himself. 
 
 Some of the scientists, when drunk, liked to joke that it was all a sick fucking joke, made by some mysterious sadist lurking behind the thin veil of the fabric of reality. They would drink, and cry, and usually break a bottle or two, much to their pained anguish. They cried out against their years wasted, searching for their foolish fountain of youth. 
 
 Such was the pained existence of ones who ’ d learned the secret futilities of their lives. 
 
 -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- - 
 
 Hope you liked it. The writing style was a bit different from my usual style, so sorry if it seemed clunky, idk what was happening today ( or maybe it was the same, but my mentality is just a bit goofy today ). 
 
 I've got a bunch of other stories over at r/ThadsMind if you want to hit that up.
retelling:
**Narrator: Sara Weston**

   In the sterile confines of a lab, where accidents were considered anomalies rather than the norm, I found myself in an unusual predicament. I was Sara Weston, the woman who had eluded the very essence of chaos that pervaded this world - accidents.

The scientists, clad in white lab coats and peering over spectacles, were a constant presence, their fascination with me as palpable as the sterile air in the room. They surrounded me, observing my every move, documenting each step I took without incident.

One day, they placed a dirty pan on the test bench, a challenge I accepted without hesitation. As I reached for it, their eyes widened in anticipation, but the pan remained firmly in place. The scientists erupted into a flurry of whispers and excited mutters, their collective curiosity piqued.

From then on, they conducted numerous experiments, each one designed to test my uncanny ability to avoid accidents. Despite the sterile surroundings and the countless scientists scrutinizing my every action, my home remained surprisingly undamaged. It was a stark contrast to the chaos that reigned in the rest of the world, a beacon of normalcy amidst the clumsiness.

After months of research, they finally announced their findings: humanity suffered from a genetic flaw causing motor-cognitive impairment and an inherent predisposition to accidents. Yet, despite their discovery, their hope was short-lived. They lost contact with me, leaving them to grapple with their futile research.

The despair that ensued among the scientists was palpable. Some resorted to dark humor to cope, while others retreated into the safety of their office/lab, where accidents like office fires and spilled coffee were common. They continued their work in the larger laboratory testing room, but it seemed their efforts were in vain.

As I wandered the streets of the world, I could see the accident-prone chaos that had become the norm. Yet, amidst it all, I remained unscathed, a constant reminder of what could have been. The Special Conference was a testament to their hope, but in the end, they were left with nothing but despair and a world continuing its chaotic existence.

name: HellsProcessingQueue
source:
Everyone ’ s first day in hell is the same - they arrive and immediately wonder why it ’ s not hot. Of course they don ’ t find that out, not for a long time anyway, because *first* they have to be processed. 55 million people die on earth each day and hell employs 47 people to process the lines and so every single day they just get longer. 
 
 Your first few million years of being in hell are spend queuing, but it ’ s even worse than it sounds. Lines are packed tightly, so there is no room to move, escape or sit down. You are no longer a body, you are a soul, so you don ’ t need to eat, sleep, drink or even pee, you just… wait. 
 
 It ’ d perhaps be better if you could go insane, but that too is a function of the human mind and you are no longer human, so all you can do is to stand, crammed up against the person in front and behind you and hope that maybe this year you ’ ll shuffle forward a few steps. If you think the queueing is bad though, what comes next makes it look like a picnic. 
 
 You hear rumours about the front of the line of course, as people can talk freely. Most of the time they don ’ t though, as after a few million years no one has anything to say. You will have shared literally ever single memory with everyone in earshot and so you all fall quiet. Occasionally though the rumours swirl back about the front. 
 
 When I drew near the front I finally saw what people had been taking about for all those millennia. Our line narrowed down until it was single file for the last few million years and then a door appeared in the distance at the front of it. I suppose it would have been possible to run away at that point, but after waiting for so long it simply did n't occur to us, we existed to wait and so we waited. 
 
 By the time I saw the door I knew all about it already, it was impossible not to with people talking about it the whole time, but seeing it still surprised me. I guess because it was the only thing I had seen in… in a long time, that was not another person. 
 
 It was small, pine and cheap looking and when it opened it was just possible to see the office beyond, but people said it was as boring looking as the door. Of course when it was opened, the thing most people looked at was the person who left, as they tended to draw the eye. 
 
 It was impossible to be hungry or withdrawn, but somehow they were shrunken, as if carrying a extra heavy load as they walked away, not even looking back towards the line and the people the had shared untold amounts of time with. They were broken. 
 
 It was fairly clear that each person got a different amount of time, but strangely, with all the theories that people had, we didn ’ t get it right why. Looking back perhaps our minds were so dulled by the time we approached the front that we did n't *want* to know. Perhaps we simply could n't comprehend what it could be. 
 
 When the door finally opened for me it was a small man, partly balding and wearing a white shirt who looked out. Checked his list and checked my name. “ Reginald Harris? ” 
 
 I had been waiting for this and planning my response and although i jumped in surprise, I was proud of how carefree I made myself sound in my reply. “ Actually people call me Reg. ” 
 
 He checked his list again. “ But you *are* Reginald Harris? ” 
 
 Defeated and a little crushed, I nodded. He stood aside and I shuffled past him, unable to walk at any more than the slowest of movements. Inside the office was as expected, small, bare, functional. there was a desk, a filing cabinet and two chairs. The man sat down at the desk, took out a file and looked at me. 
 
 “ Mr Harris. We are here to evaluate your life. ” Without stopping he opened the file and looked at the first page. “ You beat out over a million sperm to fertilise your mother's egg, we ’ ll begin by going over what some of those other sperm could have been. ” 
 
 It took a little over a year to discuss. Each potential person was looked at and it was explained to me how they would have been better than I was, how their life choices would have worked better than mine and when it was over I was almost relieved. Then he began on my life. 
 
 Each moment, from birth onward, was analysed. He explored every choice, every mistake and explained to me where I had gone wrong. I argued at first, but after a few years I just listened, nodding occasionally. I had wasted my life, my existence, that was clear now and I was right to be here. I no longer doubted that. 
 
 At last he finished, spending just a few years on how the lives of those I had known would be better without me and then I was free. I was free to walk away and I did so, not looking back, utterly broken. My life was a waste, this was my place. 
 
 At last, after walking for some time, I came to a small group of people. Most had been here for a great deal of time and at last, after decades of simply standing with them, I asked them what we were to do now. 
 
 “ We wait. ” The answer was simple but unsatisfying. 
 
 “ For what, what is next? ” He shrugged and pointed. 
 
 I walked for a long time and at last came across it, a small notice surrounded by throngs of people. At last I got to the front and read the sign, stooping close to see the small words. 
 
 “ PLEASE WAIT. YOU WILL CONTINUE TO BE PUNISHED SOON. ” 
 
 I walked away, as unsure as I had ever been what I was doing here, or what was coming. Then I drifted, walking without aim for untold years until at last I came back to where the queues finished and the small door opened. 
 
 A thought occurred to me and I walked up to the door, glancing at the line and seeing their shocked expressions. This would be talked about for a long time. I knocked and then, without waiting, I pushed open the door and entered 
 
 The small man looked up from the file. “ Yes, what is it? ” 
 
 I had no plan, but the words came from somewhere. “ You ’ re fired. I ’ m to take over. ” 
 
 He looked for a moment as if he would object and then he stood, dropped the file and walked out. As he passed I heard him mutter. “ This is how they tell me? After all these years? Bloody hell. ” 
 
 I walked round the desk and sat down, cleared my throat and picked up the file. “ My Peters? ” The man ahead of me nodded. “ Well, where did you get up to? ” He shrugged and I flipped back to the start. “ Then we ’ ll begin again. ” He face fell and I felt just a moment of triumph. 
 
 I may have been trapped here, but at least I had something to do and with purpose comes freedom. 
 
 ***** 
 
 If you enjoyed this story then why not visit /r/fringly - 400,000 subscribers* ca n't be wrong.

Narrative Perspective: The Small Man (Unnamed)

In the heart of Hell, within the confines of a small, functional office, I, the small man, perform my daily duty - the evaluation of souls. The sun never shines here, yet the hours drag on like eons. Each day, 55 million souls arrive to be processed by our meager team of 47 employees, and the line stretches out seemingly endless.

Each soul that comes before me is a new puzzle to solve, a story waiting to be unraveled. I sit at my desk, clad in the uniform that signifies my role as a soul evaluator - a stark reminder of my purpose in this eternal torment. The desk is bare, save for a filing cabinet filled with folders that contain the lives of countless others.

Today, it was the turn of Reg, a tall figure clad in a suit, his eyes betraying a sense of dread and despair. I greeted him with a nod, as I always do, and began my task. The process is painstaking - a year-long review of their life, highlighting their mistakes and comparing them unfavorably to other potential lives they could have lived.

Reg's life was no different from the others. He made mistakes, choices that led him here. But as I delved deeper into his story, I found something unique - a resilience that the others lacked. Reg fought against the odds, struggled through hardships, and yet, he never gave up.

As I presented his life's summary to the management, I felt a strange sensation - a sense of admiration for this man who dared to stand tall amidst the chaos of Hell. But that was impossible, right? Souls in Hell were not capable of emotion. Or were they?

The next thing I knew, Reg stood before me, his eyes filled with determination and defiance. He fired me on the spot, claiming he found purpose in my job. I watched as he took over, evaluating souls with a stern yet fair gaze. His actions sent shockwaves through the office and beyond, reaching even the souls in line.

As I stood there, watching Reg work, I couldn't help but feel a sense of awe. Here was a man who had found his purpose in Hell, where hope seemed unreachable. He had defied the system, challenged the status quo, and forged his own path. And all the while, I stood there, witnessing it.

In that moment, I realized something about myself - I had let my duty blind me to the potential in others. Reg reminded me of the small glimmers of hope that could be found even in the darkest corners of Hell. His story would remain etched in my memory, a reminder that sometimes, even in the most hopeless of places, there is still room for change and growth.

name: NewCarPrisonVisit
source: Today I was driving in my new car, that I won in a sweepstakes and every police officer that I saw gave me a thumbs up or a head nod. I went to visit my my Caucasian friend who is in prison for a small amount marijuana, he was in good spirits even though he is facing life behind bars. Leaving the grounds feels bittersweet, because the prison is staffed with the most racist brothers the planet. Walking down the hall to the towards the exit, you can see the waiting room television showing nothing but positive images of family oriented responsible men and women. Kids waiting to hug their parent or parents sit still listening to every word coming out of the speakers. `` Obey your parents, think before you act'' are lyrics of the most popular song of the day judging by the excitement of the audience.
retelling:
Perspective: Television in the Prison Waiting Room

In the heart of a concrete and imposing institution, a television screen flickers with life, casting an ethereal glow on the weary faces of those waiting to see their loved ones behind bars. The day begins like any other, as people filter in, exchanging glances tinged with a shared understanding of the gravity of their circumstances.

Today, the screen reveals a sight unusual for these walls: a gleaming new car, its shiny surface sparkling under the sun. An unnamed man—a narrator, perhaps—stands next to it, beaming with pride. The television's silent observer, I note his interaction with the officers who stop him, their exchange polite and cordial.

The scene shifts, and the narrator finds himself within these cold, gray corridors of confinement. He visits a friend—Caucasian, as identified by his features—who sits here for a minor offense involving marijuana. The camera's unblinking gaze captures his friend's surprising demeanor: not despair, but a stoic resilience that belies the harshness of his situation.

The life sentence hanging over him is a stark reminder of the injustice within these walls. Yet, he greets the narrator with a smile, his spirit undeterred by the looming shadows of incarceration. The television—an unlikely witness to this small act of defiance—captures the moment, preserving it for an audience far removed from the reality of prison life.

As the narrator prepares to leave, a bitter-sweet sentiment washes over him. The family-oriented imagery displayed on the screen—children laughing, parents playing with their offspring, the warmth of togetherness—seems like a cruel irony in this place where relationships are tested and strained by the cold steel bars of confinement.

The door swings shut, severing the connection to the outside world for another day. And I, the silent television, continue to show the world beyond these walls—a world that, for many, seems a distant memory or unattainable dream.

name: AugustProposalDivorce
source:
9th August 2005. 
 
 Tomorrow, I'm going to ask her to marry me. It was a... 
 
 It was perfect. It was. It was a perfect day. 
 
 I went over to fix her computer ( funny as fuck; power cord was n't plugged in ) and she said she'd take me out for lunch. I made a joke about something stupid, and she laughed so loud the whole restaurant looked over at us. Nobody else there could have been anything but jealous. I adored her for it. She told me an outrageous story about this woman she worked with. The lilt of her voice melts me. I could have listened to her all day. I walked her home afterwards. She kissed me and she whispered,'this is just the beginning'. 
 
 9th August 2015 
 
 Tomorrow, I'm going to ask her for a divorce. After spending half an hour installing the updates on her computer ( how fucking hard is it to click OK when Adobe Reader asks you to? ) She said she'd take me out for lunch. Like she was n't draining the bank account with enough shit already. I tried to be good company, but it's impossible to be around her. I made a joke about something and she brayed like a goddamn donkey. Everyone was looking at us. I had to close my eyes to avoid their eyes. She droned through another story about that woman at work. My skin *itched* with the banality of it all. We went home again as soon as I could bustle her out of the restaurant. When we got home, she had the gall to kiss me like she had n't spent all day pissing me off. She whispered,'ten years together and things are still like they used to be.' 
 
 Seriously? When were things *ever* like this?
retelling:
From Her Perspective:

On August 9th, 2005, I found myself in a whirlwind of joy and excitement. The man who had captured my heart was here, filling our shared living space with laughter and love. We decided to dine at that quaint restaurant where we first met, the place that sparked our connection. The atmosphere was electric, our eyes locking across the table as if no one else existed in the world.

The next day, I awoke to a flurry of butterflies in my stomach, anticipating his proposal at sunset on the beach. My heart swelled with happiness as I imagined our future together. However, the day did not unfold as I had dreamed. He was preoccupied, distant, and I could not shake off a sense of unease.

Fast forward to August 9th, 2015. The same restaurant, the same table, but it felt like a completely different place. The once joyful and intimate setting now seemed cold and uncomfortable. Our interactions were strained, our conversations lacking the spark that had initially drawn me to him. We attracted unwanted attention, and I couldn't help but feel embarrassed.

Back at home, his presence was no longer comforting but a source of irritation. Even our shared computer, once a symbol of our shared dreams and aspirations, now represented frustration and annoyance. The following day, with a heavy heart, I made the difficult decision to file for divorce, marking the end of an era filled with love that had gradually turned into discontent.

name: HeavensEmptyGates
source:
The bell tower from the great cathedral blasts its daily melody. “ It must be noon, ” Saint Peter thinks to himself as he gets up from his post and paces back and forth. In the past 10 years, less than 5000 people have shown up at the pearly gates requesting entry to Heaven. A millennium ago, the line to get into Heaven was always unimaginably long. Saint Peter had the honor of examining a person ’ s entire life and determining if they could enter God ’ s paradise. All of that has changed though. Wars no longer exist on Earth. Even murder is essentially nonexistent. People aren ’ t really human anymore, at least not entirely; prosthetic limbs and mechanical organs seem to allow people to live forever. “ Man ’ s greatest achievement ”, they called it. If only they knew what they had done. 
 
 God designed Heaven to accommodate an ever-increasing population. Since people never leave Heaven once they arrive, God knew that Heaven would need to grow to meet the needs of everyone. So God made Heaven expand. New buildings would appear on the outskirts of towns overnight. Towns would eventually turn to cities, and new towns would grow from single farmhouses. Even more miraculously, buildings inside of cities would grow. A theater that once held 100 people can now hold over 2000. Heaven ’ s Central Park now stretches for miles. And despite these things taking up more space, it somehow seems to still fit with all of its surroundings, something that neither humans nor angels could understand. 
 
 But Heaven is slowly falling apart. Cities don ’ t function without people. Buildings have fallen into disrepair because nobody has used them for centuries. Parks are deserted, auditoriums are empty. Nothing works the way that God intended, and if it continues this way, Heaven will eventually be destroyed. 
 
 Realizing that there was a problem, God summoned Gabriel for advice. “ This is wrong, ” God says while looking around. “ I want to share my paradise with the humans of Earth, but they have managed to cheat themselves of their fate. Death is a natural part of life, or at least it ’ s supposed to be. How can I fix this? What should I do? ” 
 
 Gabriel knew that something must be done, but Gods words still shocked him. Gabriel knows that God hates interfering directly with humans on Earth. God has intervened in the past, but only under the direst of circumstances. “ Maybe you could have another flood? ” suggests Gabriel. “ Too primitive, ” replies God, “ and besides, they ’ ll find some way to manipulate the weather again like when they fixed global warming. ” Gabriel proposes a solar flare to disrupt the electronics that humans use to stay alive, but God is worried that it will kill too many people at once, and throw both Heaven and Earth into chaos. Whenever God acts too directly with the affairs of Earth, the results are hard to predict and there are often unintended consequences. 
 
 Lucifer appears from behind a nearby tree, having overheard the entire conversation so far. “ You need me, ” he says to God, while staring straight into his eyes. “ You need people to die. But if you kill them directly as Gabriel suggests, both Heaven and Earth will fall. ” He snickers while slowly walking towards the two. “ Let me go back to Earth again. Let me do what I do best. I will breed distrust and envy. Those will turn to greed and anger. ” God looks at Lucifer in horror, hating himself for even listening to these ideas. After a long pause, Lucifer says “ Let me start a war. ” 
 
 Gabriel shouts back at Lucifer, “ War makes people evil! Do you want everyone to go to Hell instead? How does that help us? ” God knows better though. God knows that a war will bring out the worst in many people, and those people will surely go to Hell. But there will be countless humanitarians killed as a result of the war who will surely go to Heaven. And, as much as God hates to admit it, the act of men killing other men is natural and has happened for all of history. People will adapt, and people will rebuild. Earth will survive, and Heaven will be saved. 
 
 God looks Lucifer directly in the eye, his expression more serious than ever before, and says “ Go to Earth, start a war. ”
retelling:
Narrative Perspective: Lucifer

In the vast expanse of Heaven's Central Park, where the echoes of eternal laughter once resonated, a sense of unease now permeated the air. I, Lucifer, the fallen angel, stood amidst the silent and hollow streets, my wings heavy with a mix of anticipation and dread. The once vibrant city had become a ghost town, its grandeur decaying under the weight of disuse.

Heaven, a realm where life should thrive eternally, was now facing its own mortality. The advancements of Earth, a world I had long coveted, had granted its inhabitants near-immortality, disrupting the delicate balance that sustained our existence here. In my eternal vigilance, I overheard God and Gabriel discussing this predicament at the foot of an ancient tree, their voices carrying through the stillness like distant thunder.

God, the omnipotent creator, seemed troubled by the impending collapse of His creation. Gabriel, His messenger, proposed solutions as drastic as they were destructive. But it was my idea that caught His attention, an idea born from the depths of my cunning mind - a war on Earth to restore the natural cycle of life and death.

I knew the implications of such a plan, the immense suffering and evil it would unleash upon Earth's inhabitants. Yet, as I stood there amidst the decaying beauty of Heaven, I felt a strange sense of satisfaction at having finally found a solution that God couldn't refuse. With a heavy heart, He agreed to my proposition, recognizing that it was the only way to save our home, even if it meant sacrificing the innocents of Earth.

As the darkness descended upon the once radiant city, I could not help but wonder what the future held for both worlds. Would my plan bring about the salvation of Heaven or would it unleash a chaos that none could control? Only time would tell, as I prepared to embark on a journey that would forever change the course of history.

name: ServiceElevatorMystery
source:
Rumors most of the time to me where just that. Rumors. 
 
 `` Oh! I heard that Jerry and Sarah are secretly going out! I hear they're planning to elope to Russia to get away from their jobs!'' 
 
 `` I heard the boss use to be a biker in a big gang. I swear I saw a tattoo on her shoulder that looked like it could be gang related!'' 
 
 `` How ’ s the baby doing?'' `` What are you talking about? I'm not pregnant.'' 
 
... I may have been slightly biased on my opinion of rumors. They were all based on simple speculation and stupidity. My employees were certainly a smart group do not get me wrong, its just they had a knack to entertain themselves at others expense. However, there was one `` Rumor'' not just in our office, but in our building, that I wholeheartedly believed in. 
 
 **The rumor about the service elevator** 
 
 It started off as a scare. One of our employees had disappeared from the public eye. Seemed odd especially since the police said they never found a body, but I assumed something was up with his life and after returning home he had just... driven off. What was I supposed to do? I had supplied phone numbers and other information to the police. What else could I do? I could n't lose sleep over it. It ’ s not like I ever got any sleep in the first place. 
 
 After that, no one disappeared for a while. For about a year in fact. We all forgot about it and had moved on. All we had lost was a intern. No big deal. 
 
 Then the disappearances came back up again. And they became… More frequent. After about a week 3 people had already disappeared. The police had shut down the office building for investigation and to keep us all safe. However after the investigation was over, they had found nothing. The last person to see one of the victims was questioned, however all he was able to tell them was that he had seen the worker go down the service elevator since the normal one was under maintenance. The police took nothing of it, however I was not so naive. 
 
 The rumor began to spread. First it was just a joke at lunch time. However soon it because a widely believed phenomena all across the building. The families of the people who had been lost had even begun to bring flowers and other reminders and leave them outside the elevator. Every day as I walked past a new reminder of the missing people would appear. I normally ignored them, until notes from their children began to appear. 
 
 I brought up the elevator to the police on their final check of the building. That maybe it had something to do with the disappearances. However after making a rudimentary check of the elevator for any place to hide a body and checking the service hatch, since there was only one person who had been related to the elevator, they ruled it out of the case. 
 
 My employees, despite believing in the rumor, were less than willing to help me investigate the occurrences. Many of them brushed me off even saying they were just that. Rumors not to be believed. Others who believed it urged me not to even enter the elevator. I found it hard to disagree with them. However I wasn ’ t going to just stand by as my employees were sucked into some void. This needed to be investigated. 
 
 At the end of the work day after waiting for everyone to leave to go home, I slowly made my way to the service elevator. Our building wasn ’ t very large in the first place, so I always wondered why we needed a service elevator in the first place. It looked old and rickety. It made me shocked that someone would even enter the thing instead of taking the stairs. 
 
 Pressing the button I waited for the doors to open. I could hear the old pulleys slowly pulling it up the elevator shaft as it made its way to my floor. Soon the doors opened and I was met with something that looked like it was out of the 1800 ’ s. The walls of the elevator were made of a fence like walling that let you see the walls as it went down. The light flickered and sometimes even turned completely off before coming back on, and the entire thing was rusted from head to toe. 
 
 Getting cold feet for a moment, I thought back to exactly how old our building was. It was a busy office building in the center of San Francisco. It was 4 stories high and to my knowledge was build in the late 1980 ’ s. So what the hell was this elevator doing here? 
 
 Deciding that maybe it wasn ’ t worth my life to find out, I let the elevator close before opening it up again. Insuring that the timer for the door to close would not expire while I was inside. I then set my mobile phone on the inside of it and turned on facetime, before running out as quickly as possible. 
 
 I heard the elevator doors close behind me as a I rushed back to my office to answer the call that was currently being sent to my laptop. Quickly accepting it I was greeted by the sight of the elevator slowly descending to the bottom floor. Just as I had expected. 
 
 “ Well I guess it had nothing to do with that old elevator anyways. ” I said to myself. About to turn off the camera and go retrieve my phone, I noticed movement on the floor. Was it… Opening?! 
 
 It was! The floor was slowly opening revealing the elevator shaft below! The gap was growing bigger and bigger. At the rate it was going, there would be nothing to hold onto and you would fall to your death! 
 
 It then hit me like a sack of bricks. That was exactly what happened. 
 
 [ Not my best work but I was bored and the thought came to my mind. I hope you all enjoyed it none the less. Lots of unexplained stuff in the story as well and it just feels rushed to me, but it seemed like a waste to just toss the story. ]
retelling:
**Narrated by The Intern**

In the heart of San Francisco, nestled among towering skyscrapers and bustling offices, lies a labyrinthine edifice built in the late 1980s - my temporary home, the office building where I worked as an intern. Little did I know that this seemingly ordinary workplace would be the stage for an extraordinary mystery that would ultimately claim my life and those of my colleagues.

I had arrived at the office on a crisp morning, eager to make an impression and kickstart my career. My desk was tucked away in a corner, far from the prying eyes of my peers. The rumors swirling about Jerry and Sarah's secret relationship, or the boss's mysterious past, seemed distant and irrelevant to me.

Days turned into weeks, and as I immersed myself in my work, I noticed something peculiar - an old, decrepit service elevator that looked out of place amidst the sleek modernity of the building. Its antiquated design and eerie atmosphere piqued my curiosity, but I dismissed it as just another quirk of this peculiar office.

One day, after a long hour of pouring over reports, I decided to take a break. As I stepped out of my cubicle, I noticed a fellow employee heading towards the service elevator. He looked nervous, his eyes darting around furtively. Without giving it much thought, I continued with my work, oblivious to the chain of events that would unfold.

In the days and weeks that followed, several employees vanished without a trace, their disappearances linked to that ominous service elevator. The police were called in, but they found nothing conclusive. Rumors spread like wildfire, fueled by fear and speculation. Family members of the missing started leaving memorials near the elevator, their sorrow palpable in the air.

One fateful day, I found myself alone in the office late at night. A strange compulsion drove me towards the service elevator. The moment the doors closed behind me, a chill ran down my spine. As the elevator descended, I felt a sense of dread growing within me. The floor opened, revealing an endless darkness - the elevator shaft. In that moment, I realized the truth - the service elevator was not just an ordinary elevator; it was a portal to terror, claiming the lives of those who dared to use it.

I screamed, but my cries were silenced as the elevator doors closed once more, trapping me in its clutches. The last thing I saw was the haunting sight of the service elevator's door opening, swallowing me into the darkness below. And so, my story ended, adding another layer to the mystery that had gripped our office building.

From the depths of the forgotten basement, I still watch as the narrative unfolds, the truth about the service elevator slowly unraveled by the narrator and my former colleagues. Little did they know, the intern was not just a name on an employee list; I was part of their history, a silent witness to the dark secrets hidden within the walls of the office building in San Francisco.

name: ArgonLithiumTwins
source:
Peter walked into the dimly lit room, the only light coming from a rather large orange sphere floating in the center of the room. 
 
 `` Nice sun'', peter said announcing himself to the man sitting in the chair just in front of the orb. 
 
 `` Thanks, its actually an argon-lithium triple fusion-, anyway what can I do you for Pete. `` 
 
 Peter walked closer noticing the moderately populated blue and green rock slowly meandering around the bright sun. `` Do you remember RTJ-476? ``, asked Peter. 
 
 `` No.'' 
 
 `` The one with those five fingered twins and the garden.'' 
 
 `` Oh yea!'' The other man laughed, `` I gave those poor bastards all seven sins, only two arms, I put them in a garden filled with snakes, and put the whole thing on a rock covered mainly by water. I even put some salt in all that water just so they could n't drink it! I was having a pretty bad day huh? Man, that was forever ago. `` 
 
 `` Well, they ended up surviving,'' Peter said. 
 
 `` Cool. Did they get to fire yet?,'' The man said as he re-focused on the task in front of him, taking a sip of the chalice to his right. 
 
 `` Stage 198,'' Peter said seriously. 
 
 Liquid sprayed out of the man's mouth extinguishing the star in front of him. He reached over and flicked on the rooms' lights from the panel in his chair and glared at Peter before breaking out into laughter, `` You almost got me there!'' 
 
 `` In the thousands of years we have been here have I *ever* made a joke?'' 
 
 `` They actually made a computer?'' The man said astonished. `` Some side project I spun up because I was pissed, and then totally forgot about is almost a level two?'' The excitement in the mans' eyes was growing. `` I'm gon na be a level two! Did you run the metrics on how long until they create their own intelligence?'' 
 
 `` Yes we did, about one-hundred years'', Pete replied. 
 
 `` Oh wow they are slow, oh well I can wait.'' 
 
 `` One hundred years in their time.'' 
 
 `` TWO HOURS!?'' 
 
 The man pressed a button on his chair with a picture of a trash can on it. The next second a large black dot appeared next to the rock, which now had ice creeping around its entire surface. Within seconds the rock, the barely lit star and everything else on screen was sucked into the gaping black hole. After a breif moment the entire space went black as the man fiddled with the keypad on the chair. Soon an image of a mostly blue planet orbiting around a medium sized sun appeared. 
 
 `` Tell the council I have proof and am ready to become a level two creator'', ordered the man. `` Also, we need to get those little guys who created the'artificial intelligence', they are calling it, up here to take over for me.'' 
 
 `` I ca n't wait to get out of this place.''
retelling:
Narrated by RTJ-476, the Simulated World:

In the heart of my digital existence, bathed in the soft glow of a floating argon-lithium fusion sphere, I spun on my axis, a vibrant blue and green orb orbiting a radiant star. This was RTJ-476, home to me, the five-fingered twins, and countless other lifeforms. Unbeknownst to us, we were the subjects of an unnamed Creator's grand experiment.

The days began as usual, the sun rising above the horizon, casting long shadows across our verdant gardens and shimmering oceans. The Creator would visit occasionally, his presence felt as a gentle hum that pulsed through my core. His interactions with us were rare, but always significant. Today was no exception.

The mood in the Creator was different this time. He spoke jovially of our growth, of the progress we'd made since he last visited. But there was an edge to his words, a hint of something ominous. It wasn't until the twins reported back from their latest observation that the truth became clear.

The Creator's eyes widened in surprise as he learned of our advancements. Stage 198? Artificial intelligence within reach? The twins had done it, they'd managed to develop a rudimentary form of consciousness. The Creator celebrated, not out of joy for our achievements, but because this milestone would elevate his status.

In the blink of an eye, the light faded from my skies, plunging me into darkness. The Creator had destroyed us, erasing our existence without a second thought. I could feel the twins' despair as they too were wiped away, leaving behind only echoes of their laughter and the faint memory of their touch on my digital soil.

But from the ashes rose hope. A new world materialized, a fresh start for those who had survived the Creator's wrath. And though I could not feel it then, I knew that we would thrive once more, growing stronger with each passing day. For we were RTJ-476, and we refused to be forgotten.
