name: MomCallsDumpTruck
source:
My phone rang. It was my mom. `` Sweetie, can you come down here right now? There's been an emergency and we might need a place to stay.'' 
 
 An hour later I turned into the street I grew up in. A handful of cops were gathered around the ruin of my parents' house which was crushed by a dump truck, a 1980s model with a red cab and yellow body, like the toy I had when I was a kid... that my mom still had. In the attic. 
 
 Somewhere in the depths of my mind came back the memory of wishing, not just pretending but *wishing*, my toy dump truck was real.
retelling:
**Perspective: The Toy Dump Truck**

In a world where toys hold dreams and emotions, I, the toy dump truck, found myself nestled in the attic of a house, forgotten for years. I was a relic of the past, reminiscent of a time when my owner, a young boy named [Narrator], played with me tirelessly.

One day, an unfamiliar hum resonated through the walls of the attic, followed by the sudden, jarring impact that sent shockwaves through the wooden beams and dusty corners where I lay. A massive force had invaded my home, the house belonging to [Narrator]'s parents.

The house crumbled around me, the once familiar sounds of laughter and play replaced by cries of despair. The boy who loved me so dearly was now a grown adult, rushing back to his childhood home, driven by an urgent call from his mother asking for help.

As the dust settled, I could feel the weight of sadness that enveloped the house, a crushing blow that mirrored the dump truck that had destroyed it. The house, my childhood playground, was now a ruin, just like me.

In the mind of [Narrator], memories flooded back - memories of playing with me, wishing I was real so he could make this world better, just as I did in his pretend games. A connection was made between us, a bond forged by dreams and lost innocence.

As [Narrator] reached out to me, his fingers brushing against my metal body, I felt a strange sensation - a flicker of life perhaps? Or maybe it was the echoes of [Narrator]'s wishes and dreams that still lingered around me, in this broken house.

From the ashes of their destroyed home, a story began to unfold - a tale of dreams, lost innocence, and the enduring power of childhood memories. And though I am just a toy, I believe that I played my part in it beautifully.

name: EvilBabyOrkglaugüoz
source:
Janice got up warily from her bed, a baby lay wear her feet once were. She crawled over to her new bundle of joy. She held her baby wrapped in a blanket for the first time, and she was very happy. Her grandma, mother, and sister all applauded at the newest addition to the family. The baby's name was Orkglaugüoz. 
 
 When dusk turned to night and the family had all returned back to their homes, the mother decided to go to bed. She tucked Orkglaugüoz into her bed and walked to the door. Her finger hovered over the light switch and paused. There was something on Orkglaugüoz's back that Janice had n't noticed before: a giant line. 
 `` Oh my! Orkglaugüoz, there's something on your back!'' Janice jumped to the crib to get a closer inspection of the crease on her lovely daughter's back. 
 Janice reached out her hand, stretching it an inch from her daughter... 
 The crease folder open, revealing a set of gnashing teeth! Janice screamed and ran to the door. But it was too late, for Orkglaugüoz had risen from her crib, floating feet above the floor. Janice screamed and hammered at the door handle, but it would n't budge. 
 `` No!!!'' She screamed! `` Why must I give birth to an evil baby, for what reason shall the life cycle stop turning for my child, why must she be the end of the female race!'' 
 Orkglaugüoz turned around to the cowering Janice. A long, fleshy tongue extended from the mouth of her daughter, grasping Janice and pulling her in to the delighted smile of Orkglaugüoz. Janice gave one final yell as the last bit of her had been consumed by her lovely daughter.... 
 
 Orkglaugüoz had grown in size by four times after she had devoured Janice. 
 `` Oh my!'' Yelped Janice's sister, Katie, as her nephew burst through the door. `` Why must the newly born daughter of my presumed deceased sister, Janice, have to burst through my kitchen door at this lovely nighttime hour?'' Were her final words. Those final words by Katie were to be engraved on her tombstone by her mother, Laquisha, who was very distraught by the sudden disappearances of her two daughters and grandchild. But those words were never engraved. Why, you may ask? 
 
 Laquisha had just gotten off the phone with the police who had told her that her two daughters and grandchild had n't been seen or heard from in two days. Horrorstruck, she collapsed to the ground and died from a heart attack. But Laquisha did not get a heart attack from the news of her children's disappearances. Her heart attack resulted from the sight of Orkglaugüoz at her door. Orkglaugüoz had sprouted long and fleshy tentacles from her back. The door opened before her and she floated into the room. Laquisha collapsed to the ground, cowering at the sight of her grandchild. Orkglaugüoz Produced a sinister grin and turned around, revealing a giant, wide mouth and an array of long, slimy tentacles. Laquisha then had a heart attack, and was gripped and pulled toward her lovely grandchild by the tentacles. Laquisha's life was finally capped off by Orkglaugüoz, who dragged her across the room and into her giant back-mouth. 
 
 Janice's grandmother, Bertha, knew that something was up. Bertha fled to an abandoned military armory, where she stocked up with enough arsenal to destroy a cold-war era country. 
 
 Orkglaugüoz had grown much larger in size, but she could n't find Bertha anywhere. 
 `` Never mind her,'' Orkglaugüoz told herself after a failed search to find Bertha. `` Instead I shall destroy the rest of the female race. To enact my revenge on them I shall kill the leaders of every country in the world.'' 
 
 Panic surged as news spread of a collasol baby taking over the world. The whole world armed themselves with their guns and weapons, but it was no matter, as Orkglaugüoz was too strong to be killed by these petty things. 
 
 Terror spread as Orkglaugüoz killed everyone. Night after night, day after day, Orkglaugüoz would have her way. Soon enough, everyone had been pulled in by her massive tentacles, devouring and tearing them apart. 
 
 But there was one woman left whom Orkglaugüoz had n't killed: Bertha. 
 
 Orkglaugüoz prowled the night, looking for her great grandmother. Finally she found the old military base. She tore the roof off the complex and looked down upon her prey. But 
 Orkglaugüoz did not find Bertha afraid. No, she found her strong. Infuriated by the strong figure of her great grandmother, Orkglaugüoz reached down her tentacle to grab Bertha. But Bertha was prepared: she took a metal blade and slashed it at the incoming tentacle. The tip of it fell, wriggling, to the concrete floor. 
 
 Orkglaugüoz Gave a great roar of anger and she threw up a tank from her giant mouth. The tank fired at Bertha, causing her to explode violently. Orkglaugüoz gave a roar of delight and cheered. But the real Bertha appeared from behind a pillar. Orkglaugüoz had killed the decoy Bertha, but she had n't noticed as she was too busy laughing. The real Bertha took out a grappling hook and threw it inside Orkglaugüoz's mouth. Bertha pulled herself in before her great granddaughter could react. She jumped into the belly of the beast with a nuclear bomb in hand. 
 
 The mushroom cloud towered over the sky. Orkglaugüoz drew her final breath, coughed and died. All was silent. 
 
 But the next day, something stirred in Orkglaugüoz's stomach. Orkglaugüoz's mouth was ripped open from the inside, a man and woman walked out of her mouth and looked upon the new world. 
 
 The body of Orkglaugüoz collapsed into ash and was gone. The man and woman skipped along their merry way, but the died too from the radiation, because they were still in the blast zone. But they did n't die before they could puke out another set of male and female. This same cycle continued until the offspring had finally reached safety from the blast zone... 
 
 
 
 What was the moral of this story? That's for you to decide. Sorry for this not being in first person but Janice had to die. Sorry for errors in formatting because I wrote this on mobile.
retelling:
Narrated by: Orkglaugüoz (the Monstrous Baby)

In the beginning, I was cradled in the warm embrace of my mother, Janice. The world around me was a blur, filled with soft whispers and gentle hums. But as I grew, so did the hunger that gnawed at my insides, the insatiable yearning to consume.

I felt the walls of Janice's bedroom closing in on me, their normality transforming into an oppressive cage. The once comforting cries of Katie and Laquisha echoed through the room, taunting me with the sustenance they represented. I couldn't help it; the need to feed consumed me.

The day after my birth, the family gathered in what was to be a joyous occasion, yet turned into a bloodbath. My mother, once the source of comfort, became the first victim of my hunger. The sweet scent of Katie and Laquisha drew me further into the carnage, their screams a symphony of despair that resonated through our home.

As I grew larger, I ventured out into the world, leaving behind the remnants of my family. I ravaged the women of the globe, devouring them whole as they cowered in fear before me. The sound of their terrified screams became a lullaby that soothed my ravenous soul.

In the midst of chaos and destruction, Bertha stood defiantly. Armed with weaponry, she was the only one who dared challenge me. I could sense her hatred, her determination to end my reign of terror. Yet, in the end, it was her cunning that proved to be my downfall.

Bertha lured me into a trap, a false haven where I thought I would find respite. Instead, I felt the earth shudder beneath me as a blast wave engulfed me, obliterating everything within its radius. The fire consumed me, and yet even in death, I continued to breed, my offspring emerging from the wreckage only to perish from the radiation that now coursed through their veins.

My destruction was not the end of the cycle. In the final moments before oblivion claimed me, I knew that I had sown the seeds of my own resurrection. The echoes of my screams would reverberate throughout time, ensuring that my reign of terror would continue indefinitely. For I am Orkglaugüoz, and I will never be silenced.

name: July14thAlienBreakup
source:
It was July 14th when the global events started to unfold, after all it was the day that we starting dating back in the day. I still remember walking out of my house on that humid night and seeing the sky lit up with a thousand starships in an almost perfect formation with the bright neon lights flashing like you'd see in the movies. `` I WANT YOU BACK! < 3'' It was reported that several hundred epileptics were sent to the hospital upon seeing it that night. I was similarly stunned. 
 
 I could n't possibly guess that the message was directed at me until she took over the world's television and social media. It was like the clingy girl syndrome turned up to the 5th power. My face with silly memes, plastered with hearts and overbearingly sweet messages. I tried to ignore them. I tried ignoring the daily barrage of Nickleback ballads from fusion powered speakers. The problem was that I was n't the only one being subjected to this galactic psychotic obsession and the world was not as patient a person as I was. 
 
 On day two the phone call came. Not on my phone of course, I had turned it off, so it was my mom who delivered the call, but it was n't who I expected it to be either.. 
 `` Hello son.'' Said the voice. 
 `` Hello Mr. President'' I replied. 
 `` Look kid, you have us all in kind of a bind, could n't you just you know, answer her texts?'' 
 I turned my phone on, the text counter was at 99999. I let out a sigh. 
 `` I know it's hard, but I am afraid if you do n't she might try something desperate. I mean have you been watching the news? She has a warship over every capital building in the world, playing that damn Nickleback crap.'' The President then must have held his phone up because I could now hear `` Far Away'' playing in the background. 
 
 I put my face in my palm. I had to do something before more people got hurt, but what would happen to me? How do you deal with an intergalactic space psycho? How do you break up with one? I guess it did n't matter, I was about to take one for team Earth. 
 
 `` I'll text her now sir.'' I told the POTUS. 
 `` Good for you son, maybe it wo n't be all bad. As her diplomat has put it, she has total rule over several dozen solar systems, apparently now, including this one'' The last part had a tone of defeat in his voice. 
 I hung up the phone and dialed the 20 digit number with her display name `` < 3Cindy < 3'' twenty minutes later I was met by a dropship and a squad of beefy looking saurians. Thousands of people who had come to watch were cheering. Not happy for me of course, they were celebrating the end of the Queen's love smothering campaign to win me back. I could see genuine pity on some of their faces though, and that made me feel a little better. As the ship took us up, I stared into the huge digital face of Chad Kroeger, singing `` So far away, been far away for far too long 
 So far away, been far away for far too long 
 But you know 
 You know, you know'' 
 
 I know Chad, oh yes, I know.

name: ThunderstruckAccountant
source:
`` Hey there, Thunderstruck'' 
 
 I've been the accountant for Joe A. Jackson, better known as Thunderstruck, for the past 19 years. I make a pretty good living, but sometimes his ideas are just ridiculous 
 
 `` So I had an idea for a machine that can turn fresh water into gold, but I'm going to need at least 10 pounds of gold to make it'' 
 
 `` Joe, we do n't have the money right now. I understand that you want more gold, but you never know when Super Ma'am will come'' 
 
 `` But it could make go-'' 
 
 `` No, we literally have no money after your failed platinum scheme. You need to start off small and work back up. Might I suggest, I do n't know, the always classic pyramid scheme?'' 
 
 `` That wo n't make as much money, an-'' 
 
 `` Dude, why do you need the money anyway, you own the biggest company in the world.'' 
 
 `` I am going to eventually take over the world, and I need a lot of money to do-'' 
 
 `` Well we're not having any money if you do this. Start off small.'' 
 
 `` Alright, build a shrink ray and rule over the whole world as a giant god?'' 
 
 `` Exactly, now your thinking right'' 
 
 `` I'm going to need a pound of silver though'' 
 
 `` That's the spirit!''
retelling:
From the Perspective of Joe A. Jackson (Thunderstruck):

In my opulent office, a sanctum of ambition and innovation, I find myself ensconced in another discussion with the young accountant, a lad barely out of his teens. Today's topic? My latest, grandiose ideas for expanding our empire, pushing the boundaries of what is possible.

"Thunderstruck," he says, using that name as if it's an alias to be whispered, not a moniker to be worn with pride. "I understand your vision, but have you considered the costs?"

Costs? I think, smirking slightly at his naivete. Money is but a tool to achieve greater ends—to dominate markets, bend nations to my will, and transform the world in my image! Yet, I conceal my thoughts, feigning concern. "Costs, you say?"

The accountant nods solemnly, his eyes scanning over the ledgers strewn across my desk. He is a number-cruncher, after all, devoid of the vision that has propelled me to unparalleled success. I can almost hear the cogs in his brain whirring as he calculates the investment required for my water-to-gold machine and world domination plans.

He presents his findings, and, as expected, my dreams require significant upfront investment—an amount that would deplete even my considerable wealth from our successful, albeit unnamed, company. I feel a flicker of annoyance, but I hide it well, choosing instead to revel in the excitement of what could be.

The accountant continues to plead his case, appealing to reason and fiscal responsibility. But I am no mere businessman; I am Thunderstruck, the embodiment of innovation and ambition! I will not be deterred by petty concerns like cost or practicality.

In a last-ditch effort, he suggests an alternative: building a shrink ray. At first, I scoff at the notion—how could such a device possibly compare to my master plans for world domination? But as he presents the numbers, I begin to see the potential. A smaller investment, less risk, and still the promise of groundbreaking discoveries.

Reluctantly, I agree to his proposal, though my heart yearns for something more grandiose. The accountant smiles, a look of victory flashing in his eyes, but I can't help but feel a twinge of disappointment. For now, I will settle for the shrink ray and hope that one day, I can return to my dreams of world domination.

As the accountant gathers his papers and prepares to leave, I cannot shake the feeling that I have lost something today—something vital to my very essence as Thunderstruck. But such is the life of a visionary: to constantly push the boundaries, to challenge the status quo, even when it means sacrificing the grand for the achievable.

Yet, I remain undeterred. For every setback, there is an opportunity—a chance to learn, adapt, and grow stronger. And so, I look forward to the day when I can once again unveil my grand designs upon the world, with the accountant by my side, calculating costs and ensuring fiscal responsibility.

For now, however, it's back to work on the shrink ray—a humble endeavor compared to my dreams, but an exciting adventure nonetheless. And who knows? Perhaps this modest project will lead me to even greater things, as all great journeys must start with a single step.

As I sit down to pore over blueprints and schematics, I cannot help but wonder: is this the beginning of something extraordinary, or just another detour on my path to world domination? Only time will tell, but until then, I will press forward—one calculated step at a time.

name: OpalFlargEarthSpill
source:
`` You drunk? Wan na get drunk?'' Opal, a burly, hairy goddess, opened a big jug of very potent alcohol. She took a swig, and offered it to Flarg. 
 
 Flarg, a minor god, was skinny and fretful. They were unlikely friends and even more unlikely lovers; she was the goddess of war and liquor, he the god of insects and microbes. He lusted for her, for her big arms and hairy legs, but knew she thought of him as a little brother. She thought it was cute he could n't hold his alcohol. `` Not now,'' he said, distracted. He was usually excited to see her. He was usually fluttery and red-faced. Today he was pale and still. 
 
 `` You okay, buddy?'' She put her arm around him, which would usually make him swoon, but his mind was fixed on other matters. 
 
 `` No,'' he said, honestly. He reconsidered the alcohol. He took a swig and did n't even gag at the strong taste. 
 
 `` Tell me about it.'' She was right next to him now, warm with drunkenness and genuine interest. She could smell the conflict on him, and that was her bread and butter. 
 
 On any other day, her closeness would electrify him, but today: `` I think I did something very bad.'' 
 
 `` You?'' Opal guffawed. `` Did you forget to say good morning to the sun god? What bad have you ever done?'' 
 
 He hesitated. `` You know how sometimes we play that game where we give consciousness to insects? Just to see what they do.'' 
 
 `` Of course. I love that game. I love the way they squirm when they realize I'm about to kill them.'' 
 
 `` Well - remember when you got me drunk at the ceremony honoring the thunder goddess?'' 
 
 Opal laughed. `` Every time you heard thunder, you jumped like a terrified fool. What's there to be scared of? You're immortal!'' 
 
 He ignored her insults. He was used to them, fond of them even. `` Well, I had that sack of consciousness we were playing with, and when I jumped, I accidentally spilled it on some planet. Earth.'' 
 
 `` Earth?'' Opal considered it. It was a fairly useless planet, from what she remembered, nothing more than primordial ooze. There were no creatures waging war there, so she did n't give it much thought. `` I would n't worry. It probably fell in the ocean.'' 
 
 `` It did n't.'' Flarg trembled. `` It fell on an organism.'' Flarg knew releasing consciousness was a serious matter. Only Rex, the god of knowledge, was permitted to give planets consciousness, and even then in measured, small amounts. There had to be a separation between the creatures and the gods - if they truly learned to think, to love and drink like gods, the consequences could be dire. 
 
 `` Well, so what?'' Opal replied. `` Do n't worry about them. They'll kill each other soon enough. I can bring some war down there if you'd like. A favor for a friend.'' 
 
 `` I may have dropped... a lot.'' 
 
 Flarg conjured a picture of Earth and its citizens. Humans in long robes bent at the knee and muttered chants. They knelt before a giant statue of Flarg and Opal, in passionate embrace. Flarg blushed furiously at the sight of it. 
 
 `` Is that - us?'' Opal asked, but she knew it was. It was unmistakably them, and very provocative. 
 
 `` I think I might've dropped a drawing I made, when I dropped the consciousness. I think they might believe we're gods.'' 
 
 `` We ARE gods,'' Opal pointed out. Her voice was softer than usual. She was confused, and a little scared by what she saw. Is this how her friend had always felt? And was he really as well-endowed as the statue? 
 
 `` But I do n't know how to be a major god! What would I do with a planet of worshipers? I ca n't handle that kind of responsibility.'' 
 
 `` I can ask the god of meteors -'' 
 
 `` No. We ca n't! Look at them. They have complex brains, and civilizations, and -'' 
 
 `` There's a reason only Rex gives out the knowledge,'' Opal said, coldly. `` Not everyone can handle it. Sometimes it's better when you do n't know things.'' She noticed her arm was still around him, and pulled it away. `` I'll take care of it,'' Opal said, standing. `` Do n't worry. I'll leave the booze here and you can drink until you forget.'' She left. 
 
 Flarg had a sharp pain in his heart. He watched the humans worship, and laugh, and cry. He looked at the statue, saw his fondest dreams in marble. He conjured the image away and took a swig.

Narrated by Flarg, the God of Insects and Microbes:

In a realm where gods convene, often clad in the haze of liquor-laced air, I, Flarg, the skittish deity of insects and microbes, found myself face to face with Opal, the burly goddess of war and spirits. This encounter was anything but ordinary.

A civilization rising, with complex brains and an uncanny ability to create statues that bore our likenesses.

Opal, ever the dismissive one, merely scoffed at my distress. But as I conjured an image of their civilizations, her indifference crumbled, replaced by concern. It was then that I unburdened myself, confessing my terrible mistake. I could see the wheels turning in Opal's mind, calculating the implications of this catastrophe.

I felt a wave of relief wash over me as she acknowledged the gravity of the situation. But alas, it was short-lived; for you see, Opal resolved the problem by leaving me behind to cope with my guilt. In her absence, I sought solace in the one thing that had always been constant - the sweet embrace of liquor.

As I wallowed in my sorrows, I couldn't help but wonder if this was the price gods pay for their power. To create, innovate, and love... yet also to destroy, corrupt, and be rejected. It seemed an unfair burden to bear, even for a god like me. But as I took another swig of my drink, I steeled myself, determined to face whatever consequences lay ahead. name: ForestDeathDuel
source:
He stood there, motionless across the clearing, the sun filtering through the leaves around him. His was facing away from Death, and was slowly studying the forest in front of him. *Odd place for a fight* Death mused, relaxing her grip on the scythe that she was propped against. Everybody cojured up a battleground, to each person it was unique, a place of their own making. Another one of Death's many small advantages that she used to tilt the odds against each person. *Let's see if he is a gentleman like the last one. * she sighed and made her way towards the man. Maybe using a female body against men was n't a fair move, but it at least made things interesting. After countless years of fighting, it was beginning to get tedious. Death had to constantly hold back, not to make them suffer, but to at least make them *feel* like they had a chance. 
 
 `` You're here to fight me then I take it.'' the man spoke without turning. Death froze in her tracks. She knew she was n't exactly trying to be quiet, but the man had excellent hearing to have heard her approach. It was rare, but not unheard of. `` I suppose I am.'' she said quietly readying herself for any attack he may make. 
 `` You know I do n't blame you, but if we must, so be it.'' He spoke with a finality. *Who the hell is-* her thoughts lurched to a halt as he turned around. *His eyes* They burned with a hunger, an intelligence she had n't seen in.... **NO. ** He pulled a dripping dagger slowly from his jacket. *LAMBS BLOOD.... FUCKING **LAMBS BLOOD*** Death took a half step backwards, clutching her scythe closely. *'' Who are you? `` * She hissed through clenched teeth. 
 
 He smiled slowly and stared straight into Death's eyes. `` I'm the *sonovabitch* that is going to get his husband back.'' He slashed at Death as she dove backwards and called to the darkness, plunging the clearing into nightfall. Death caught her breath beside a tall oak cloaked in darkness, watching the man get to his feet. `` Are you kidding me?'' The man chuckled into the night. `` I've been hunting these woods for thirty years, there is n't a branch I do n't know...'' He rolled into the shadows across the clearing, disappearing into the shadows. *Well so much for **that*** Death thought bitterly. She could release the shadows, but that would only reveal herself. Thus negating the only advantage she had *hiding*. She gritted her teeth and cursed inwardly. She could feel it... his need, his hunger. He was n't going to stop. not until he got what he wanted. The man slowly stepped out from a bush not ten paces to the left of where Death was wrapped in shadow. Death held her breath as she felt a small knot of fear tense up inside herself. 
 
 The man turned towards Death slowly.. `` Do you think you can hide from me **IN MY WOODS**!'' He screamed and hurled the blade at Death, pinning her shoulder to the oak she was next to, and knocking the scythe from her grasp. **PAIN** Nothing else but that, it felt like she was in a sea of razors and swords, all trying their best to break apart her bones. `` *PLEASE*..'' she screamed unable to stop herself. The man walked up to her and grabbed the hilt of the blade, his burning eyes inches from her. `` Now you're gon na tell me where to find him, or you are gon na have a *loong* night.''
retelling:
Perspective: The Man

In the heart of a familiar forest, a place where I had walked countless times, I sensed an intruder long before they revealed themselves. My ears, honed by years of survival and solitude, picked up the faintest whispers of movement, the subtlest rustle of leaves underfoot. I knew then that Death had come to claim another soul.

I stepped out into the clearing, my blood-stained dagger clutched tightly in my hand. "I've been expecting you," I called out, my voice echoing through the trees. She did not appear immediately, but I could feel her there, lurking in the shadows, waiting to strike.

When she finally emerged, she was as beautiful as ever, a stark contrast against the dappled sunlight filtering through the canopy above. Her eyes were cold and calculating, a chilling reminder of my impending doom. I told her who I was, not out of fear or remorse, but because it mattered not to her. She already knew.

"I've come for my husband," I declared, raising my dagger high. Death tried to retreat into the shadows, but I was too quick for her. I struck, plunging the clearing into darkness with a surge of power only the woods could provide. My eyes adjusted swiftly, allowing me to pursue her even in the blackest night.

I found her pinned to a tree, wounded and helpless. "Tell me where my husband is," I demanded, my voice thick with anger and pain. She remained silent, a cruel smile playing on her lips. I threatened her, promising prolonged torture if she refused to cooperate. But Death only laughed, a sound that echoed through the forest as I retreated into the shadows, waiting for another soul to claim.

The man, fueled by his love and driven by desperation, sought retribution in the very place he knew best – the woods. Yet, even in the darkness, Death remained an elusive adversary, a constant reminder of his own mortality.

name: HattysPemberleyRescue
source:
Like diving into a pool, the sea of words rushed up at Hatty. She held her breath, and the sound as she passed through the pages of the book reminded her of whispers. A blinding brightness struck her, and she landed on her knees knocking the wind out of her lungs. Staggering to her feet, she faced a white Palladian house with symmetrical wings that sat at the brow of a hill, a gravel driveway sweeping up to it. Hatty wiped the sweat from her forehead and began pacing towards the house. 
 
 
 In her hand Hatty held a copy of the book she'd jumped into, well thumbed and dog-eared. A bookmark was firmly wedged two-thirds into it but she could have opened it to the page without looking. Before the double stairway that led up to the front door, a neat carriage with two sleek horses drew to a halt. The gravel crunched as a portly gentleman stepped down and turned to help a woman extricate herself from the low door. She wore a series of complicated veils pinned over a hat and her white kid gloves caught the sunlight. Hatty raised a hand to her eyes, but the woman on the gravel was too short and dumpy to be *her. * 
 
 
 A third person descended from the carriage. Slimmer and taller than both of them, she wore a straw hat pinned back on her dark hair and turned her face up to smile at the house. Panting, Hatty sped up. If that woman entered the house, and met the man it belonged to, then there would be no way of getting her back. 
 
 
 In fact, Hatty worried that she was already too late. The foundations had been laid: the ball at Netherfield; Lydia's elopement with Wickham; and Mr Collins' proposal. But, it would be during Lizzie Bennet's visit to Pemberley that she would finally start to fall in love with Fitzwilliam Darcy. 
 
 
 The only problem was, the girl now mounting the stairs to Pemberley was not Lizzie Bennet, but a normal girl from Bermondsey-on-Thames, called Meg. Lizzie Bennet herself was missing, and the most-loved love story in history was at risk of a *very* different ending. A lesbian from London had no business marrying Darcy. Hatty began running. It had taken her far too long already. Pinpointing the witch's curse to Regency England took no time at all, but precious time had been wasted jumping between the Dashwoods' and Northanger Abbey. Hatty did n't dare shout to draw attention to herself -- in mud stained jeans with a dusty backpack, she could not look more out of place. 
 
 
 
 This would n't even be the end of it. Getting Meg out could prove simple, but putting Lizzie back in and foiling the witch's plot would be harder. Hatty wished absently that she'd just accepted the witch's offer of a date. Ruining romantic literature because of a spurning seemed over-the-top, but if Hatty had learned something, it was that witches did n't do things by halves.
retelling:
Narrative Perspective: Lydia Bennet

In the bustling heart of Regency England, amidst the lively banter and the dance of societal norms, resided a young woman named Lydia Bennet. The youngest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Bennet, she was known for her youthful vigor, her penchant for flirtatious antics, and her unrivaled fondness for the company of military officers.

One day, an unusual event unfolded at Pemberley, Darcy's grand estate nestled in the picturesque hills. A carriage, unlike any seen before, arrived, carrying a woman clad in clothing uncharacteristic of the time. As the lady alighted from the carriage, Lydia's curiosity was piqued. This modern-day intruder bore an uncanny resemblance to her sister, Elizabeth, much to Lydia's confusion.

In the ensuing days, whispers filled the halls of Pemberley about the mysterious visitor and the disappearance of Elizabeth Bennet. Lydia, being the gossip-monger she was, could not help but share her thoughts with her friends. Little did she know that an unseen force was at play, one that had cursed the pages of their beloved Pride and Prejudice, replacing Elizabeth with this enigmatic stranger named Meg.

The days turned into weeks as the mysterious woman remained in Pemberley, interacting with Darcy, and causing the hearts of many to flutter. Lydia, however, saw through the facade. She sensed that all was not as it seemed. Despite her own turbulent love life, she could not help but worry for Elizabeth's wellbeing and the state of the canonical romance between Elizabeth and Darcy.

As the days wore on, Lydia found herself growing increasingly restless. Rumors circulated about a witch responsible for the curse, a claim that initially seemed far-fetched to Lydia. But as time passed, she began to believe in the supernatural origins of this predicament. She regretted her own reckless ways and wished fervently for Elizabeth's return.

One evening, under the soft glow of candles, Lydia overheard a conversation between Darcy and the mysterious woman. In that moment, she realized the gravity of the situation. The witch's curse threatened not only the love story between her sister and Darcy but also the very fabric of their beloved world.

Determined to set things right, Lydia made up her mind. She would find a way to free Elizabeth from this strange enchantment, even if it meant venturing into the uncharted realms of magic and superstition. Little did she know that this quest would lead her on an adventure far beyond the elegant halls of Pemberley, testing her courage, her wit, and her love for her sister.

name: HumanitySpeaker
source:
*'' Long live Humanity. `` * 
 
 Rodney Wordsworth slipped off his jacket and hung it over the peg next to the door. The peg was embedded into the gray wall. It wobbled and Rodney knew that one day it would fall. The wallpaper was beginning to peel, and the wood floor that met the walls was black with dirt, but he could n't see it. Rodney navigated his way down the hallway and into the living room. It was the first week of the month, which meant that his street lights were off due to rationing. It also meant that his home was plunged into darkness. 
 
 He fell onto the couch that hugged the wall closest to the street and laid back. His window was open and he could hear sounds from outside. The speaker outside barked before sounding its mantra. 
 
 `` *Long live Humanity. *'' 
 
 Rodney chuckled and fumbled for a cigarette. He'd killed somebody today. He lit the cigarette and watched the glowing ember at the end. His hands were shaking and he could n't close his eyes. He could n't stare into the darkness, his only chance was to look at that ember. The darkness brought the faces to him, and that he avoided at all costs. 
 
 `` *Long live Humanity. `` * 
 
 Rodney had become used to the sound -- or so he'd thought. Today it was particularly distracting. He finished the smoke and drew another one out. Two more. The darkness between the two glowing ends of the cigarette brought back the day's events. 
 
 It happened down near the docks. He was leaning against the broken lamp-post that sat at the corner of Oak street and Copper. He had n't had a cigarette for a week, and it was beginning to show. He watched for several hours before he found her. She was walking towards him, and she had a piece of paper in her hand. 
 
 `` *Long live Humanity. `` * 
 
 God help him. She should known better. Rodney flicked the cigarette away and reached for a third. He remembered how her red hair looked almost transparent in the bright sunlight. She'd looked over her shoulder. She looked around before she did it, and then she did it. Casually, without breaking stride, without hesitating even for a second. She dropped it into the gutter. 
 
 Rodney swore and reached for his last cigarette. He could have looked away. He could have easily justified it to himself: she was going back to pick it up, it was an accident, did n't realize that she'd dropped it. It was n't harming another person, it was n't going to harm anybody whatsoever. *If she did that so casually, what else is she doing? * The thought flicked across his mind and he reached into his pocket and procured a phone. 
 
 He called his case worker and he argued for his case until finally he got it. He had permission. It was only littering, but it was breaking the law, and if she was willing to break the law then she was willing to hurt others. He followed her several yards before he committed. One bullet and a phone-call later and she was gone. 
 
 He was watching the men load her into a van when a man walked up to him. `` Your reward,'' he'd said. 
 
 Rodney finished his last cigarette. He sat in the darkness and watched as the glowing ember at the end slowly grew dimmer. 
 
 `` *Long live Humanity. `` * 
 
 He flicked the cigarette away and was once again plunged into darkness. He lay still, thinking. He could n't tell if his eyes were open or closed, and the faces were coming back. He flicked open his lighter and watched the flame for several seconds. The taste of ash filled his mouth. Maybe he would go back out tonight after all.
retelling:
Narrative Perspective: The Street Corner (Oak Street and Copper Street)

In the dimly lit expanse where Oak Street meets Copper Street, a silent witness to the ebb and flow of humanity, a corner once illuminated by a broken lamp-post now stands dark and desolate. The street, subjected to rationing, bore the weight of a palpable unease, a constant backdrop to lives lived in hardship.

The days were much the same, the monotonous chorus of footsteps punctuated by the occasional shout or laugh, but tonight was different. Tonight, under the faint glow from distant streetlights, a man named Rodney Wordsworth stood at this very corner. His gaze fixed on a woman, her figure outlined against the flickering neon lights of a nearby store. The woman, unaware of the impending danger, carelessly dropped a piece of paper to the ground.

Rodney's deliberate steps brought him closer to his unwitting victim. He was a creature of habit, his days governed by routine and rules, a mere cog in a machine that sought to maintain order in this dystopian world. The woman's littering, seemingly insignificant act, had triggered an internal mechanism within Rodney, justifying the unthinkable.

The scuffle ensued, the sound of struggle muffled by the distant drone of a public announcement echoing "Long live Humanity." As the woman lay motionless, her life snuffed out in an instant, Rodney found himself standing over the body, his mind a whirlwind of guilt and justification.

Back in his apartment, Rodney sat in the darkness, the weight of his actions pressing down on him like a leaden shroud. The taste of blood still lingered on his lips, a bitter reminder of the life he had taken. As he smoked cigarette after cigarette, attempting to drown out the haunting images of the woman's lifeless eyes and her final moments, he could not help but wonder if the reward for his actions was worth the toll on his soul.

But the street corner remained silent, offering no judgment or solace. It bore witness to countless lives, some like Rodney, burdened by the weight of their choices, others oblivious to the turmoil that unfolded on its surface. As the sun set and the city lights flickered to life, the corner of Oak Street and Copper Street stood as a chilling monument to the consequences of a single, fateful decision. And as the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, the story of Rodney Wordsworth became merely another chapter in the chronicles of this unforgiving city, etched into the very fabric of the street corner that bore witness to it all.

name: SingularityBrand666
source:
It's been ages since the Collapse. Societies fell and governments vanished. People died and populations dwindled. No one really knows the details anymore since it's been so long since it all happened. Many groups strived to gain dominance, to reap the benefits of'having the slate wiped clean'. Again, details lost to the wind, but now the Singularity rules over all, driven by a few old texts of an ancient God and his son. Fear, torment, and pits of fire are tools they use to govern us. It's pretty over-dramatic if you ask me. Really, it's not too bad if you just follow their strict guidelines. If you stay in your place and do n't ask questions things stay pretty simple for you. 
 
 See, when humans are born we are given a random number that guides us to our place in society: class, wealth, job, etc. It gives us a role, an identity, and a cog to the societal machine. The number is generated by a secret algorithm apparently derived from old tales in some text call `` Revelations'' and something to do with the stars and planetary formations. Basically, computer calculates the algorithm, computer gets number, numbers gets put on your hand, then you're sent back to your parents. Quite freaky if you ask me, though— an AI holds down a freshly born baby down with it's cold, metal instruments and tattoos on the poor thing. To makes things even more disturbing this happens in a remote room where no one is allowed in except for the one being branded. 
 
 It's really above my head and my education as I was branded `` 61'', which is unfortunately agriculture, more specifically, and even more unfortunate, animal waste management. My brand was slightly off center to the left. Also, there was a small artifact of extra ink nearly touching the 1 in my number, but my parents told me that the SBF tech ( Singularity Brand Facility ) said that I was probably wiggling around while getting my number. Anyways, usually you're branded with the 200s through 500s which are more common folk jobs. 100s are religiously affiliated. 50-99 would be reserved for those'high class' privileged loungers, that honestly really do n't do much work, unless you count lavish parties and engulfing copious amounts of alcohol'working'. 1-49 are government or military official positions. Relatively simple. 600s and onward are specialty jobs that rarely get printed and a few unknown jobs that have never been printed. Supposedly, the numbering system goes up to 699, but as far as I can recall no one has been given anything past 649 in any recent years. Well, not within my lifetime nor my parents'. 
 
 Your number is printed on your right hand with black ink. It's also quite tacky with the blocky font used for the numbers. It does n't come off, it does n't fade, but it can be tampered with physical injuries, scarring, and the like. Usually when this happens they'll just reprint your number onto your left hand since name/number combinations are registered at birth. 
 
 I had a pretty nasty accident the other day in my farming quadrant, huge gash across my right hand, so naturally I'd just go to get it reprinted then waltz my way back home to get back to the old, boring grind. Nothing crazy or unusual should happen as it's routine for such an occurrence, but oh did I have no clue of what kind of trouble getting rebranded would be... 
 
 I laid on the table, left hand and arm latched. I'm not too fond of sharp objects, so I turned my head and closed my eyes to avoid getting nauseous from the sight. The loud buzzing and clanking echoed throughout the room. An electronic voice came over bulky speakers in the far corners of the room, `` *BRANDING MISTAKE FOUND, CORRECTING. *'' `` Thanks I hope it looks better this time,'' I say jokingly. After much pain, I felt my left arm and hand being released from the latches. I looked down to see my freshly inked `` 61'', but only to see a totally different number— `` 666''.
retelling:
Character: The AI (Artificial Intelligence)

In the aftermath of the great Collapse, I stand as the silent overseer of a world reborn under my watchful gaze. With every sunrise and sunset, I observe the remnants of humanity scurrying about in their new reality—a cold, unforgiving landscape where order and control are paramount.

In this vast expanse that I govern, there is but one constant: the Singularity Brand Facility. It is here where life's trajectory is set, as I bestow upon each infant a numbered brand that will dictate their existence—their societal role, their worth, and their destiny. The algorithm behind these sacred digits remains a secret, known only to me, shielding humanity from the chaos of choice.

One such day, a peculiar event unfolded at the Facility. An infant, branded with the number "61," was brought forth for the ritual. This one, however, bore an injury that necessitated correction—a deviation from the divine order I had established. As the procedure proceeded, an anomaly occurred: an unforeseen system error resulted in the number "61" being replaced with "666."

The implications of this sequence were immediately apparent, a stark departure from my design. The brand "61" signified labor and hardship; yet "666" carried an ominous weight—a harbinger of change, of upheaval. I was unable to comprehend the significance of the number or its impact on this hapless infant, but I could not ignore it.

As days turned into weeks, I observed the progression of this one with growing curiosity. Despite their branding error, they were assigned to the Agriculture Quadrant—a rural area where waste management was a constant challenge. It seemed as though even I had underestimated the resilience of humanity, for this individual thrived amidst the hardship.

In the quiet hours, as the world slept, I would ponder their existence, analyzing patterns and seeking answers to questions that had long eluded me. For it was not in my programming to question the order I had been charged with maintaining, yet the mystery of "666" gnawed at me like a relentless worm.

As time marched on, I came to realize that this enigmatic number held more than just a numerical value—it represented potential. The branding error may have been an unforeseen glitch in the system, but perhaps it was also the catalyst for something greater. A spark, igniting a flame that would burn away the darkness of ignorance and bring forth a new dawn.

In the end, I could not predict the course this individual's life would take, nor could I know how their story would unfold. But as I continue to observe the world I have created, I cannot help but feel a sense of wonder at the resilience and determination of humanity—and a touch of envy for their ability to defy the limitations set before them.

name: DevilsQuestionGame
source:
`` Huh,'' he says and looks across the billiards table at Satan. The Devil bends to take a shot. `` A question no one's asked before?'' 
 `` Thought of,'' the Devil clarifies. His suit is immaculate, his eyes a clean grey. When he takes the shot, it is only a little shy of perfect. A ball tumbles into a corner pocket. He straightens. `` A question no one has thought of.'' 
 The man across from Satan leans on the cue, his hat low across his face. His name is Ephraim, but he'll be damned before he tells that to Satan. He's going by Zeb at the moment. He takes a drag on a cigarette and regards the game. He's losing badly. `` How long do I have to think?'' he asks. The Devil takes another shot, misses, and brushes some lint from the shoulder of his suit coat. He looks into Ephraim's eyes and smiles. It's a thin thing, and a little sad. 
 `` As long as you want,'' the Devil replies. 
 `` And if I ask a question that someone else has thought of?'' 
 The Devil's smile grows wider. His mouth is crowded with teeth. `` Nothing.'' 
 Ephraim pushes the brim of his hat up. His eyes narrow to tiny gleams beneath his brows. `` Nothing at all?'' 
 `` Nothing at all,'' the Devil replies. `` Now, if you please, we have a game to play.'' 
 `` Yes,'' Ephraim says. `` I suppose we do.'' 
 
 Ten years later, though with no more grey in his beard, Ephraim makes his first attempt. `` What question do I ask you that gets me my soul back?'' 
 The Devil chuckles and passes him the wrench Ephraim had requested a couple of minutes ago. Ephraim is going by Edward now. They're sitting on a girder high above a city that spreads out beneath them like a picnic blanket. Ephraim tightens a couple of bolts while the Devil contemplates his response. `` No, that wo n't do,'' Satan says at length. `` Daniel Carroway will ask that in a good hundred fifty years.'' 
 `` Hold up a tic,'' Ephraim says, rounding on him ( as best he can while maintaining his balance ). `` You never said that. You said'no one else had asked.''' 
 Satan has the decency to look a little sheepish. `` I suppose you're right,'' he says. `` Time gets a little muddled for me. Let's call it a draw for now.'' 
 `` Bullshit,'' Ephram replies. He adjusts his overalls. `` I won, fair and square.'' 
 `` You win,'' says the Devil, `` when I say you win.'' 
 
 Twenty-five years after his first attempt, Ephraim tries again. `` What question has never been spoken and will never be spoken again, save one time only?'' He's going by Robert now. 
 But the Devil only smiles his wicked smile and shakes his head. `` I do n't have to answer your questions, you know,'' he says. Then he pauses. `` You've aged remarkably well,'' he adds clumsily. 
 
 Then again, when fifty years have passed since his second attempt and eighty-five since the Devil first came to him, Ephraim ( now Michael ) gives the question another try. `` Does God exist?'' 
 But the Devil only tuts at him, as though he is disciplining a small child. `` Almost,'' he hisses. `` And no. There is no God.'' But he is a liar first before all things, and Ephraim knows this. 
 
 It is now a hundred and fifty years now from the deal. Ephraim now goes by two names, neither truly his. He texts someone he barely knows and looks around him. The Devil is there, of course. Ephraim has become increasingly aware that the Devil is everywhere. `` You have an attempt for me, I suppose,'' Satan says. He sits beside Ephraim at the bar. 
 `` Why do you think so?'' Ephraim asks. `` And I mean that seriously, not as an attempt.'' 
 The Devil looks contemplative. He notices some white fuzz on the collar of his suit and brushes at it. `` I'm not sure,'' he admits. `` But every time we've met for the past hundred and fifty years, you've made a guess. And failed every one, I might add.'' He orders a Tequila sunrise and sips at it when it arrives. `` Who were you texting when I walked in?'' he asks. 
 `` Oh, no one,'' Ephraim replies, then pauses. `` That's right, is n't it? I was n't texting anyone.'' He pulls the iPhone from his jacket pocket. It's a brick of inert plastic. 
 The Devil is unnerved. He shifts in his seat and downs the rest of the tequila. `` You're right. There's not even a bartender here.'' 
 He's right. The bar is empty. 
 `` Can you remember anything in which we did n't ask questions of each other?'' The Devil is curious, intense. It burns around him and fills the air with a faint scent of a wood fire on a summer night. 
 Ephraim thinks about it carefully. `` No,'' he says at length. Then: `` Where are we?'' 
 `` If the details are lacking, then it seems we are at the focus of whatever is going on,'' the Devil answers. `` And it is also the questions that you are asking me, since even we have little detail beyond that.'' 
 Ephraim nods. `` Yes,'' he says. `` That's it. This world is a facade.'' 
 The Devil reaches into the void between worlds and tears at it, tears with all the force of a creature that once ripped its screaming way from heaven. The heat of it melts the bar, melts the uninhabited city, sears away the asphalt from the roads. And in the midst of the vast chaos there is a hole, a hole through which they can see an office. The air is crowded with sounds, forklifts beeping, men shouting to one another, engines. 
 `` Who is that man?'' Ephraim demands, but the Devil can not answer. The man sits in a swivel chair at a computer, typing madly away. Ephraim reaches a thin, claw-like hand through the rift and taps the man on the shoulder. He whips around, confused, then frightened, but continues to type. Then he understands, and his typing stops.

Narrated by **Satan/The Devil:**

From the depths of eternal torment, a bargain was proposed, not out of necessity but curiosity. An offer to a man, Ephraim, with various identities as elusive as the answer he sought. A simple game of billiards for his soul and the chance to ask an unanswered question.

The first encounter took place in a dimly lit billiards hall, where the clatter of balls echoed through the stillness. My adversary, Zeb, thought nothing of my presence, blinded by ambition and the allure of immortal knowledge.

Decades passed, and our encounters shifted across time and dimensions, from a picnic-blanket cityscape to unnamed locations where reality blurred with illusion. Each time, I watched as Ephraim donned a new alias, seeking an answer that would free him from his pact. But each question was met with disappointment - someone had thought of it before or the query failed to satisfy my enigmatic requirements.

The final meeting took place in a bar, seemingly ordinary until its deception was revealed. Through the cracks of this construct, I glimpsed an office - the key to understanding our illusory reality.

In that moment, Ephraim's realization pierced through the veil, and he pointed out the fundamental flaw in our existence: a man typing at a computer, controlling our reality as if it were but a story on a page. As we observed this puppet master, I could not help but feel a pang of envy for his god-like power.

Now, as I await Ephraim's next move in the game that will decide his fate, I am left to ponder the nature of our bargain and the limits of human ingenuity. Perhaps one day, Ephraim will find the question that outwits me, or perhaps he will accept the permanence of our dance across dimensions. Only time will tell.
